items.answerText: Victoria University of Wellington has conferred an honorary degree on a distinguished astrophysicist in a recent graduation ceremony. Professor Couch is a distinguished astrophysicist who has __played/led/done/found__ a crucial role in the discovery that the Universe is expanding at an accelerating rate, a finding which led to the lead scientists being awarded a Nobel Prize in Physics in 2011, which he attended in recognition of his contribution. In his research, Professor Couch uses large ground-based and space-based telescopes to observe galaxy clusters, __which/who/they/those__ are the largest Structures in the Universe. He is also involved in a number of national and international committees overseeing the management of these telescopes. __In addition to/As a result of/Instead of/Regarding__ his own research activities, Professor Couch has worked to support young researchers and provide public comment on astronomy internationally.
items.fullText: Victoria University of Wellington has conferred an honorary degree on a distinguished astrophysicist in a recent graduation ceremony. Professor Warrick Couch received the honorary degree of Doctor of Science for his remarkable contribution to our knowledge of galaxies and dark energy. Professor Couch is a distinguished astrophysicist who has played a crucial role in the discovery that the Universe is expanding at an accelerating rate, a finding which led to the lead scientists being awarded a Nobel Prize in Physics in 2011, which he attended in recognition of his contribution. In his research, Professor Couch uses large ground-based and space-based telescopes to observe galaxy clusters, which are the largest Structures in the Universe. He is also involved in a number of national and international committees overseeing the management of these telescopes. In addition to his own research activities, Professor Couch has worked to support young researchers and provide public comment on astronomy internationally.
items.beginnerText: Victoria University gave a special degree to a great scientist. The scientist is Professor Warrick Couch. He got a Doctor of Science degree. He helped us learn about galaxies and dark energy. Professor Couch helped find out that the Universe is getting bigger faster. Because of this, some scientists won a Nobel Prize in 2011. He went to the Nobel Prize event because he helped with the discovery. Professor Couch uses big telescopes to study galaxy clusters. Galaxy clusters are the biggest things in the Universe. He also helps manage these telescopes with other groups. Besides his research, Professor Couch helps young scientists. He also talks about astronomy to the public.
items.intermediateText: Victoria University of Wellington recently awarded an honorary degree to a notable astrophysicist. Professor Warrick Couch received an honorary Doctor of Science degree for his significant contribution to understanding galaxies and dark energy. As a distinguished astrophysicist, Professor Couch played a key role in discovering the accelerating expansion of the Universe. This discovery led to the award of the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2011 to the lead scientists; Professor Couch attended the ceremony in recognition of his contribution. In his research, Professor Couch utilizes large telescopes, both on Earth and in space, to observe galaxy clusters (the largest structures in the Universe). Furthermore, he participates in several national and international committees that manage these telescopes. Beyond his research, Professor Couch supports young researchers and provides expert commentary on astronomy to the international community.

He believed that art, or __at least/in part/by contrast/actually__ his art, was for everyone. Soon, Haring opened a store which he called the Pop Shop, which he hoped would attract a broad range of people. items.fullText: Keith Haring began as an underground artist, literally. His first famous projects were pieces of stylized graffiti drawn in New York subway stations. Haring travelled from station to station, drawing with chalk and chatting with commuters about his work. items.beginnerText: Keith Haring started as an artist in the subway. He drew graffiti in New York subway stations. Haring went to different stations and drew with chalk. He talked to people about his art. His drawings helped him make his special style. He drew so much, up to 40 drawings each day. Soon, he became famous and made money. Later, art galleries wanted to buy his art. His paintings became very expensive. But Haring did not like this because he thought art should be for everyone. So, Haring opened a store called the Pop Shop. He wanted many people to come to his store. Some street artists did not like this. They said Haring was 'selling out'. But the Pop Shop changed how people thought about art and business.
items.intermediateText: Keith Haring began his career as an underground artist. His initial famous works were stylized graffiti in New York subway stations. Haring moved between stations, using chalk to draw and discussing his art with commuters. These early drawings helped him develop his signature style. He became very productive, creating up to 40 drawings daily, which quickly led to fame and financial success. Soon, galleries and collectors wanted to purchase Haring's full-sized pieces. Although the prices of his paintings greatly increased, this conflicted with Haring's belief that art should be accessible to all. Therefore, he opened a store called the Pop Shop, aiming to attract a diverse audience. While the Pop Shop was controversial among some street artists, who accused Haring of 'selling out', it ultimately changed perceptions of the relationship between art and business.

items.title: #3 Intelligence Comparison
items.answerText: Comparing the intelligence of animals of different species is difficult, how do you compare a dolphin and a horse? Psychologists have a technique for looking at intelligence that __does/can/do/did__ not require the cooperation of the animal involved. The relative size of an individual's brain is a reasonable indication of intelligence. Comparing __across/to/through/with__ species is not as simple as generally expected. An elephant will have a larger brain than a human has simply because it is a large beast. __Instead/Then/Because/Otherwise__ , we use the Cephalization index, which compares the size of an animal's brain with the size of its body. Based on the Cephalization index, the brightest animals on the planet are humans, __followed/follows/follow/following__ by great apes, porpoises and elephants. As a general __rule/theory/principal/principle__ , animals that hunt for a living (like canines) are smarter than strict vegetarians (you don't need much intelligence to outsmart a leaf of lettuce). Animals that live in social groups are always smarter and have larger EQ's than solitary animals.
items.fullText: Comparing the intelligence of animals of different species is difficult, how do you compare a dolphin and a horse? Psychologists have a technique for looking at intelligence that does not require the cooperation of the animal involved. The relative size of an individual's brain is a reasonable indication of intelligence. Comparing across species is not as simple as generally expected. An elephant will have a larger brain than a human has simply because it is a large beast. Instead , we use the Cephalization index, which compares the size of an animal's brain with the size of its body. Based on the Cephalization index, the brightest animals on the planet are humans, followed by great apes, porpoises and elephants. As a general rule , animals that hunt for a living (like canines) are smarter than strict vegetarians (you don't need much intelligence to outsmart a leaf of lettuce). Animals that live in social groups are always smarter and have larger EQ's than solitary animals.
items.beginnerText: It is hard to compare how smart different animals are. For example, how can you compare a dolphin and a horse? Psychologists have a way to study intelligence. The animal does not need to help with this method. The size of an animal's brain can show how smart it is. Comparing animals is not easy. Elephants have big brains because they are big animals. So, we use the Cephalization index. This compares the size of the animal's brain to the size of its body. The smartest animals are humans, apes, porpoises, and elephants. Animals that hunt are usually smarter than animals that only eat plants. You don't need to be smart to eat a leaf! Animals that live in groups are smarter than animals that live alone. They also have larger EQ's.
items.intermediateText: It is challenging to compare the intelligence of different animal species, such as dolphins and horses. However, psychologists have developed a technique to assess intelligence without needing the animal's cooperation. The size of an animal's brain can indicate its intelligence. Yet, comparing intelligence across species is more complex than it seems. For instance, an elephant's brain is larger than a human's simply due to its larger body size. Therefore, we use the Cephalization index, which compares brain size to body size. According to this index, humans are the most intelligent, followed by great apes, porpoises, and elephants. Generally, animals that hunt, like canines, are smarter than vegetarians, as it doesn't require much intelligence to eat plants. Also, animals living in social groups tend to be smarter and have higher EQ's than solitary animals.

items.title: #4 Longevity
items.answerText: People are living longer and this longevity is good news for sales teams. It results in a much more __precise/usual/right/honest__ customer base for them to work from. Why we are living longer is not the issue for anyone __involved/mixed/concerned/linked__ in drawing up plans to market a product. What they focus on is the fact that there are now more age groups to target, which means that a sales pitch can be re-worked a number of times to more exactly fit each one. For example, __rather than/while/by/even when__ referring simply to 'adults', there are now 'starting adults', 'young adults' and 'established adults'. __Similarly/Even/While/Really__ , markets no longer talk about 'children', but tend to refer to a fuller range of categories that includes 'kids', 'tweens', 'pre-teens' and 'teenagers'. We now have a very diverse population in terms of age, and that can only be a __bonus/favour/promise/desire__ for business.
items.fullText: People are living longer and this longevity is good news for sales teams. It results in a much more precise customer base for them to work from. Why we are living longer is not the issue for anyone involved in drawing up plans to market a product. What they focus on is the fact that there are now more age groups to target, which means that a sales pitch can be re-worked a number of times to more exactly fit each one. For example, rather than referring simply to 'adults', there are now 'starting adults', 'young adults' and 'established adults'. Similarly , markets no longer talk about 'children', but tend to refer to a fuller range of categories that includes 'kids', 'tweens', 'pre-teens' and 'teenagers'. We now have a very diverse population in terms of age, and that can only be a bonus for business.
items.beginnerText: People live longer now. This is good for sales teams. They can find the right customers more easily. It doesn't matter why people live longer when planning to sell something. Sales teams care that there are more age groups now. So, they can change their sales talk to fit each group better. For example, they don't just say 'adults.' Now, they say 'starting adults,' 'young adults,' and 'established adults.' Also, they don't just say 'children.' They say 'kids,' 'tweens,' 'pre-teens,' and 'teenagers.' There are many different ages of people now. This is good for business.
items.intermediateText: Because people are living longer, sales teams benefit from this increased longevity. This leads to a more clearly defined customer base. The reasons for increased lifespan are not important for product marketing strategies. Instead, marketers concentrate on the wider variety of age groups. As a result, sales pitches can be modified to target each group more effectively. For instance, the term 'adults' has been broken down into 'starting adults', 'young adults', and 'established adults'. Likewise, instead of 'children', markets now use a range of categories like 'kids', 'tweens', 'pre-teens', and 'teenagers'. Consequently, this diverse age range within the population presents a valuable advantage for businesses.

items.title: #5 Push and Pull
items.answerText: People move to a new region for many different reasons. The __motivation/accommodation/combination/abbreviation__ for moving can come from a combination of what researchers sometimes call 'push and pull __factors/generators/ideas/settings__ ' — those that encourage people to leave a region, and those that attract people to a region. Some of the factors that motivate people to move __include/mean/indicate/behold__ seeking a better climate, finding more affordable housing, looking for work or retiring from work, leaving the __congestion/configuration/concoction/conjunction__ of city living, wanting a more pleasant environment, and wanting to be near to family and friends. In reality, many complex factors and personal reasons may __interact/intercept/intercede/intersperse__ to motivate a person or family to move.
items.fullText: People move to a new region for many different reasons. The motivation for moving can come from a combination of what researchers sometimes call 'push and pull factors ' — those that encourage people to leave a region, and those that attract people to a region. Some of the factors that motivate people to move include seeking a better climate, finding more affordable housing, looking for work or retiring from work, leaving the congestion of city living, wanting a more pleasant environment, and wanting to be near to family and friends. In reality, many complex factors and personal reasons may interact to motivate a person or family to move.
items.beginnerText: People move to new places for many reasons. They may move because of ‘push and pull factors’. ‘Push factors’ make people want to leave. ‘Pull factors’ make people want to move to a new place. People may want a better climate. They may want cheaper housing. They may look for a job or retire. Some people want to leave busy cities. They may want a nicer place to live. Some people want to be closer to family and friends. Many things can make a person or family move.
items.intermediateText: People relocate to new regions for various reasons. Their motivation often involves a mix of what researchers term 'push and pull factors'. Push factors encourage people to leave an area, while pull factors attract them to a new one. Common reasons for moving include seeking a more favorable climate or more affordable housing. People may also move to find work or to retire. Others leave to escape the congestion of city life, desiring a more pleasant environment, or to be closer to family and friends. Ultimately, a combination of complex factors and personal reasons usually motivates a person or family to move.

items.title: #6 Language Extinct
items.answerText: At the moment, there are between six and seven thousand languages in the world. According to linguists, fifty percent of these are in danger __of becoming/to become/became/have become__ extinct. The speed of language loss has accelerated over the past few decades because businesses that need to communicate with a range of people from other cultures __prefer/select/fancy/must__ to employ more widely used languages, such as English, Chinese, or Spanish. This attitude is understandable, but it means that many local languages are dying out before anyone __has had/would have/have/having had__ the opportunity to study them. According to linguists, some of these languages could reveal a great __deal/size/load/capacity__ of useful information about language learning and cognitive development. In addition, a local language that has been built on the local culture contains words and phrases that express that culture; lose the language and you arguably may lose the culture, too. items.fullText: At the moment, there are between six and seven thousand languages in the world. According to linguists, fifty percent of these are in danger of becoming extinct. The speed of language loss has accelerated over the past few decades because businesses that need to communicate with a range of people from other cultures prefer to employ more widely used languages, such as English, Chinese, or Spanish. This attitude is understandable, but it means that many local languages are dying out before anyone has had the opportunity to study them. According to linguists, some of these languages could reveal a great deal of useful information about language learning and cognitive development. In addition, a local language that has been built on the local culture contains words and phrases that express that culture; lose the language and you arguably may lose the culture, too. And finally, historians will argue that a language contains evidence of a region's history and should, for that reason alone, be preserved.
items.beginnerText: Today, there are about 6,000 to 7,000 languages. Linguists say that half of them may disappear. Languages are disappearing faster now than before. This is because companies want to talk to many cultures. They use common languages like English, Chinese, or Spanish. This makes sense, but local languages are dying. We don't have time to learn about them. Linguists think these languages have important information. They can teach us about language learning and how our brains grow. Also, a local language shows the local culture. It has words that show that culture. If the language disappears, the culture might, too. Also, historians say languages hold history. So, we should keep them safe.
items.intermediateText: Currently, there are approximately six to seven thousand languages spoken worldwide. Linguists estimate that fifty percent of these languages are at risk of extinction. The rate of language loss has increased in recent decades. This is largely because businesses prefer to use widely spoken languages such as English, Chinese, or Spanish for international communication. While this preference is understandable, it results in the loss of many local languages before they can be studied. Linguists suggest that these languages could provide valuable insights into language learning and cognitive development (how our brains develop). Furthermore, local languages often reflect the local culture through unique words and phrases; therefore, losing a language can also mean losing a culture. Finally, historians contend that languages contain historical evidence of a region and should be preserved for this reason.

items.title: #7 Southern Cone
items.answerText: In the southern cone especially, from Venezuela to Argentina, the region is rising to overthrow the legacy of external domination of the past centuries and the cruel and destructive social forms that they have helped to establish. The __mechanisms/merchants/metabolism/machinery__ of imperial control — violence and economic warfare, hardly a distant memory in Latin America — are losing their effectiveness, a sign of the shift toward independence. Throughout the region a vibrant __array/sequence/flow/direction__ of popular movements provides the basis for a meaningful democracy. The indigenous populations, as if in a rediscovery of their pre-Columbian legacy, are much more active and influential, particularly in Bolivia and Ecuador. These developments are in part the result of a phenomenon that has been observed for some years in Latin America: As the elected governments become more formally democratic, citizens __express/extent/export/expose__ an increasing disillusionment with democratic institutions. They have sought to construct democratic systems based on popular participation rather than elite and foreign __domination/detection/illustration/determination__ .
items.fullText: In the southern cone especially, from Venezuela to Argentina, the region is rising to overthrow the legacy of external domination of the past centuries and the cruel and destructive social forms that they have helped to establish. The mechanisms of imperial control — violence and economic warfare, hardly a distant memory in Latin America — are losing their effectiveness, a sign of the shift toward independence. Washington is now compelled to tolerate governments that in the past would have drawn intervention or reprisal. Throughout the region a vibrant array of popular movements provides the basis for a meaningful democracy. The indigenous populations, as if in a rediscovery of their pre-Columbian legacy, are much more active and influential, particularly in Bolivia and Ecuador. These developments are in part the result of a phenomenon that has been observed for some years in Latin America: As the elected governments become more formally democratic, citizens express an increasing disillusionment with democratic institutions. They have sought to construct democratic systems based on popular participation rather than elite and foreign domination .
items.beginnerText: In the southern part of South America, from Venezuela to Argentina, things are changing. The area wants to end the control from other countries that happened in the past. This control caused bad social problems. Ways that powerful countries controlled others, like violence and economic war, are not working as well now. Latin America remembers these things well. This shows the area is becoming more free. Now, Washington has to accept governments it wouldn't have before. All over the area, many popular groups are helping to build a real democracy. Native people are acting like they are finding their history from before Columbus again. They have more power, especially in Bolivia and Ecuador. These changes are partly because of something seen in Latin America for years. The governments that people vote for are becoming more democratic. But people are not happy with how democracy is working. They want to build democracies where everyone can join in, not just rich people or foreign countries.
items.intermediateText: In the southern cone, particularly from Venezuela to Argentina, the region is working to overcome the historical external domination and the resulting destructive social structures. The methods of imperial control, such as violence and economic warfare, remain a vivid memory in Latin America. These methods are becoming less effective, indicating a move towards independence. Consequently, Washington is now obliged to accept governments that previously would have faced intervention or retaliation. Across the region, various popular movements are forming the foundation for a significant democracy. Indigenous populations are increasingly active and influential, especially in Bolivia and Ecuador, seemingly rediscovering their pre-Columbian heritage. These developments are partly due to a trend observed in Latin America for some time: as elected governments become more formally democratic, citizens are growing increasingly disillusioned with democratic institutions. They aim to create democratic systems founded on widespread participation, rather than dominance by elites and foreign powers.

items.title: #8 Global Heating

items.fullText: Three degrees does not sound like much but it represents a rise in temperature compatible with the global heating that occurred between the last ice age, some 15,000 years ago, and the warmth of the eighteenth century. When Earth was cold, giant glaciers sometimes extended from the polar-regions as far south as St Louis in the US and the Alps in Europe. Later this century when it is three degree hotter glaciers everywhere will be melting in a climate of often unbearable heat and drought, punctuated with storms and floods. The consequences for humanity could be truly horrific; if we fail to act swiftly, the full impact of global heating could cull us along with vast populations of the plant and animals with whom we share Earth. In a worst-case scenario, there might - in the 22nd century - be only a remnant of humanity eking out a diminished existence in the polar-regions and the few remaining oases left on a hot and arid Earth.
items.beginnerText: Three degrees may not seem like a lot. But it means the Earth's temperature will rise. This is like the warming that happened after the last ice age, about 15,000 years ago. It is also like the warming in the 1700s. When Earth was cold, big glaciers reached far. They went as far as St Louis in the US and the Alps in Europe. Later in this century, it will be three degrees hotter. Glaciers will melt. The weather will be very hot and dry. There will also be many storms and floods. This will be very bad for people. If we don't act fast, global heating will hurt us. It will also hurt many plants and animals. In a very bad case, in the 2100s, only a few people might be left. They will live in cold areas and a few wet places on a hot, dry Earth.
items.intermediateText: Three degrees may seem like a small change. However, it represents a temperature increase similar to the global warming that occurred between the last ice age (about 15,000 years ago) and the 18th century. During the ice age, when Earth was much colder, large glaciers stretched from the polar regions to places like St Louis in the US and the Alps in Europe. Later this century, with a three-degree increase, glaciers will melt, leading to unbearable heat and drought, along with severe storms and floods. The consequences for humanity could be devastating. If we do not act quickly, the full impact of global warming could destroy us and many plants and animals. In a worst-case scenario, in the 22nd century, only a few humans might survive. They would live in polar regions and the few remaining oases on a hot and dry Earth.

items.title: #9 Cloth-making
items.answerText: About 10,000 years ago, people learned how to make cloth. Wool, cotton, flax, or hemp was first spun into a thin thread using a spindle. The thread was then woven into a fabric. The earliest weaving machines __probably/doubtless/possible/possibility__ consisted of little more than a pair of sticks that held a set of parallel threads, called the warp, while the cross-thread, called the weft, was inserted. Later machines called looms had rods that separated the threads to allow the weft to be inserted more __easily/precise/accuracy/accurate__ . A piece of wood, called the shuttle, holding a spool of thread, was passed between the separated threads. The basic __principles/role/foundation/criteria__ of spinning and weaving have stayed the same until the present day, though during the Industrial Revolution of the 18th century many ways were found of __automating/slower/faster/existing__ the processes. With new machines such as the spinning mule, many threads could be spun at the same time, and, with the help of devices like the flying shuttle, broad pieces of cloth could be woven at great speed.
items.fullText: About 10,000 years ago, people learned how to make cloth. Wool, cotton, flax, or hemp was first spun into a thin thread using a spindle. The thread was then woven into a fabric. The earliest weaving machines probably consisted of little more than a pair of sticks that held a set of parallel threads, called the warp, while the cross-thread, called the weft, was inserted. Later machines called looms had rods that separated the threads to allow the weft to be inserted more easily . A piece of wood, called the shuttle, holding a spool of thread, was passed between the separated threads. The basic principles of spinning and weaving have stayed the same until the present day, though during the Industrial Revolution of the 18th century many ways were found of automating the processes. With new machines such as the spinning mule, many threads could be spun at the same time, and, with the help of devices like the flying shuttle, broad pieces of cloth could be woven at great speed.
items.beginnerText: People started making cloth about 10,000 years ago. They spun wool, cotton, flax, or hemp into thread. They used a spindle to do this. Then, they wove the thread into fabric. The first weaving machines were simple. They used sticks to hold threads called the warp. Another thread, the weft, went between them. Later, looms were made. Looms had rods to make it easier to put the weft in. A shuttle held thread on a spool. It passed between the threads. Spinning and weaving are still done the same way today. But in the 1700s (the Industrial Revolution), new ways were found to make it faster with machines. New machines like the spinning mule spun many threads at once. The flying shuttle helped weave cloth very quickly.
items.intermediateText: Around 10,000 years ago, humans discovered how to create cloth. Materials like wool, cotton, flax, or hemp were initially spun into thin threads using a spindle. Subsequently, these threads were woven into fabric. Early weaving machines likely consisted of simple structures, such as sticks, that held parallel threads, known as the warp, while the weft (the cross-thread) was inserted. Later, looms were developed. Looms used rods to separate threads, which allowed easier insertion of the weft. A piece of wood, called the shuttle, carrying a spool of thread, was passed between the separated threads. Although many processes were automated during the Industrial Revolution of the 18th century, the basic principles of spinning and weaving have remained constant. New machines, for example, the spinning mule, enabled the simultaneous spinning of numerous threads. Furthermore, devices like the flying shuttle allowed for the rapid weaving of wide pieces of cloth.

items.title: #10 Electricity
items.answerText: It would be very hard to imagine life without electricity. Most of the appliances and machines that are used in homes, offices and factories are powered by electricity and this equipment __helps to improve/helps improving/help improved/help improve__ people's overall quality of life. For that reason, the wider provision of electricity supplies is a critical factor in reducing global poverty __levels/ranks/stages/contributions__ . To meet the needs of users around the world, the global consumption of coal has risen more quickly __since/in/at/for__ 2000 than any other fuel. For countries that do not have their own supply of natural energy resources, coal has become an essential __means/factor/course/aspect__ of producing power. On a global scale, coal is currently used to fire power stations and produces 40% of global electricity. This __figure/sum/volume/total__ is very likely to increase, and predictions are that by 2030 coal will fuel 44% of world's electricity.
items.fullText: It would be very hard to imagine life without electricity. Most of the appliances and machines that are used in homes, offices and factories are powered by electricity and this equipment helps to improve people's overall quality of life. For that reason, the wider provision of electricity supplies is a critical factor in reducing global poverty levels . To meet the needs of users around the world, the global consumption of coal has risen more quickly since 2000 than any other fuel. For countries that do not have their own supply of natural energy resources, coal has become an essential means of producing power. On a global scale, coal is currently used to fire power stations and produces 40% of global electricity. This figure is very likely to increase, and predictions are that by 2030 coal will fuel 44% of world's electricity.
items.beginnerText: It is hard to think about life without electricity. Many things in our homes, offices, and factories use electricity. These things make our lives better. So, giving more people electricity is very important to help reduce world poverty. Since 2000, people around the world have used much more coal than other fuels. This is to get the energy they need. If countries don't have natural energy, they use coal to make power. Coal is used in power stations to make electricity. Today, coal makes 40% of the world's electricity. This amount will likely grow. By 2030, coal may make 44% of the world's electricity.
items.intermediateText: It is difficult to imagine life without electricity. Most appliances and machines in homes, offices, and factories rely on electricity. These tools improve people's quality of life. Therefore, providing more electricity is a key factor in lowering global poverty. Since 2000, the world's use of coal has increased faster than any other fuel source. For countries lacking their own natural energy resources, coal has become a vital way to produce power. Globally, coal is used in power stations to generate 40% of the world's electricity. This percentage is expected to rise. Predictions indicate that coal will fuel 44% of the world's electricity by 2030.

items.title: #11 Climate
items.answerText: Climate is the word we __use/estimate/predict/describe__ for weather over a long period of time. The desert has a dry climate because there is very little rain. In 1852, the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India measured Everest's height as 29,002 feet above sea level. This measurement was accepted for over a century. In 1955, the height was slightly adjusted by 26 feet to 29,028 (8,848 m). The mountain was officially named in 1865 after Sir George Everest. He was the British Surveyor General from 1830 to 1843 who mapped the Indian subcontinent. However, he was hesitant to have the peak named after him. He believed the mountain should keep its local name, which was common practice for geographical societies. Before the Survey of India, other mountains were considered the world's highest. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, Chimborazo in the Andes was thought to be the highest. However, at 20,561 feet (6,310 m), it is much lower than Everest. About thirty other Andean peaks and several Himalayan peaks are taller. In 1809, Dhaulagiri (26,810 feet; 8,172 m) was declared the highest, but it was replaced in 1840 by Kanchenjunga (28,208 feet; 8,598 m), which is now the third-highest. Everest has been the highest for the past 150 years, although its position has faced some challenges.

items.answerText: Decision making is central to the management of an enterprise. items.fullText: Decision making is central to the management of an enterprise. The manager of a profit making business has to decide on the manner of implementation of the objectives of the business, at least one of which may well relate to allocating resources so as to maximize profit. A non-profit-making enterprise (such as a department of central or local government) will be making decisions on resource allocation so as to be economical, efficient and effective in its use of finance. All organizations, whether in the private sector or the public sector, take decisions which have financial implications. Decisions will be about resources, which may be people, products, services or long-term and short-term investment. items.beginnerText: Making decisions is very important for running a company. A manager of a business that wants to make money must decide how to reach the business goals. One goal is to use resources to make the most profit. A non-profit group (like a government office) makes choices about using money well. They want to be cheap, work well, and get good results. All groups, both private and public, make choices that affect money. These choices are about resources like people, goods, services, or investments. Choices also include what activities to do and how to do them. Most choices will involve thinking about money and costs.
items.intermediateText: Decision making is essential for managing any enterprise. For a profit-making business, the manager must decide how to implement the business's objectives. One key objective often involves allocating resources to maximize profit. A non-profit enterprise, such as a government department, makes decisions about resource allocation to ensure economical, efficient, and effective use of funds. All organizations, whether private or public, make decisions with financial implications. These decisions concern resources, including people, products, services, and both long-term and short-term investments. Decisions also relate to activities, specifically whether and how to carry them out. Furthermore, most decisions at some point require consideration of financial matters, particularly costs.

items.title: #49 Crop Losses

items.fullText: As demand for food and competition for land rises, it is vital that crop losses are limited . Chemical protection has provided effective control of crop losses in recent years. Alongside chemical fertilizers and improved crop genetics, it has helped to increase crop yields dramatically over the last six decades. However , there is now a need to develop complementary alternatives, and researchers from the Rural Economy and Land Use Program have been exploring the potential of -- and barriers to -- alternative pest management approaches. 'Alternatives to chemical pesticides are needed because overuse of them leads to pesticide resistance and affects biodiversity and water quality,' says Dr Alastair Bailey. items.beginnerText: The need for food is growing. There is also more competition for land. So, it is very important to limit crop losses. Chemical protection has helped control crop losses lately. It has increased crop yields a lot in the last 60 years. This is because of chemical fertilizers and better crop genetics. But now, we need other choices. Researchers are looking at alternative pest management. They are studying its potential and problems. Dr Alastair Bailey says, 'We need alternatives to chemical pesticides. If we use too much, pests become resistant. It also hurts biodiversity and water quality.' He adds, 'EU rules are stricter. Many pesticides are being taken off the market. items.intermediateText: As the demand for food increases and competition for land intensifies, limiting crop losses is crucial. In recent years, chemical protection has effectively controlled these losses. Combined with chemical fertilizers and improved crop genetics, this has significantly increased crop yields over the past six decades. However, there is a growing need for complementary alternatives. Researchers from the Rural Economy and Land Use Program are exploring the potential and barriers of alternative pest management approaches. Dr. Alastair Bailey states, 'Alternatives to chemical pesticides are necessary because their overuse leads to pesticide resistance and negatively impacts biodiversity and water quality.' He also notes that 'Stricter EU regulations are causing many pesticide products to be withdrawn. Therefore, complementary approaches are required to reduce pesticide use and maintain the effectiveness of the remaining valuable pesticides, in order to sustain food production systems.'

items.title: #50 Underground Houses
items.answerText: Underground houses have many advantages over conventional housing. Unlike conventional homes, they can be built on __steep/geometric/flat/overhead__ surfaces and can maximize space in small areas by going below the surface. They are also wind, fire, and earthquake resistant, providing a secure and safe environment in extreme weather. One of the greatest benefits of underground living is energy __efficiency/ratio/consistency/renewal__ . The earth's subsurface temperature remains stable, so underground dwellings benefit from geothermal mass and heat exchange, staying cool in the summer and warm in the winter. This saves around 80% in energy costs. By __incorporating/intriguing/initiating/inventing__ solar design this energy bill __can be reduced/has reduced/can reduce/has been reduced__ to zero, providing hot water and heat to the home all year round.
items.fullText: Underground houses have many advantages over conventional housing. Unlike conventional homes, they can be built on steep surfaces and can maximize space in small areas by going below the surface. In addition, the materials excavated in construction can be used in the building process. Underground houses have less surface area so fewer building materials are used, and maintenance costs are lower. They are also wind, fire, and earthquake resistant, providing a secure and safe environment in extreme weather. One of the greatest benefits of underground living is energy efficiency . The earth's subsurface temperature remains stable, so underground dwellings benefit from geothermal mass and heat exchange, staying cool in the summer and warm in the winter. This saves around 80% in energy costs. By incorporating solar design this energy bill can be reduced to zero, providing hot water and heat to the home all year round.
items.beginnerText: Underground houses are better than normal houses in some ways. They can be built on hills. They can also make small spaces bigger by going underground. Also, builders can use dirt from the ground to build the house. Underground houses use less material because they are smaller. It also costs less to fix them. They are safe from wind, fire, and earthquakes. So, they are a safe place when the weather is bad. One of the best things is that they save energy. The ground under the earth stays the same temperature. This helps the houses stay cool in summer and warm in winter. This saves about 80% on energy bills. If you use solar power, you can save even more. You can get free hot water and heat all year.
items.intermediateText: Underground houses offer several advantages compared to conventional housing. Unlike regular homes, they can be constructed on steep slopes and maximize space in compact areas by utilizing subsurface space. Furthermore, materials dug up during construction can be reused in the building process. Because underground houses have a smaller surface area, they require fewer building materials and result in lower maintenance costs. Additionally, they are resistant to wind, fire, and earthquakes, which provides a secure environment during extreme weather conditions. A significant benefit of underground living is energy efficiency. The earth's subsurface temperature remains consistent, allowing underground homes to benefit from geothermal mass and heat exchange; they stay cooler in the summer and warmer in the winter. This results in energy savings of approximately 80%. By adding solar design elements, the energy bill can be reduced to zero, providing hot water and heating throughout the year.

items.fullText: In the developed world, home appliances have greatly reduced the need for physical labour. Fewer people need to be involved in tasks that once left them little time to do much else. For example, the word processor and email have, to a great extent , replaced the dedicated secretarial staff that briefly flourished with the rise of the typewriter. At one time all copies were made with manual scribes, carefully duplicating what they read. Then we had carbon paper. Then photocopiers. Then printers. Then the requirement for physical copy reduced. An entire stream of labour appeared and disappeared as technology advanced. We freed ourselves of one kind of work; we just replaced it with another.
items.beginnerText: In rich countries, machines in homes have cut down on hard work. Now, fewer people have to do jobs that used to take up all their time. For example, computers and email have mostly replaced secretaries. Secretaries were popular when typewriters became common. Long ago, people copied texts by hand very carefully. items.intermediateText: In developed countries, household appliances have significantly lessened the need for physical labour. Consequently, fewer individuals are required to dedicate their time to tasks that previously consumed most of their day. For instance, word processors and email have largely replaced the secretarial staff. These staff members were in high demand when typewriters became common. Initially, all copies were created by scribes who manually duplicated texts. Subsequently, carbon paper was introduced, followed by photocopiers and printers. As technology advanced, the necessity for physical copies decreased. An entire form of labour emerged and then disappeared. While technology freed us from certain tasks, it simultaneously introduced new forms of work.

items.title: #52 Big Buildings
items.answerText: The desire to build big is nothing new. Big buildings have been used to show off power and wealth; to honor leaders or religious beliefs; to stretch the limits of what's possible; and even as simple __competition/spite/division/compliment__ among owners, families, architects, and builders. Some of the most __dramatic/dreadful/derivative/dreary__ buildings of the past include the pyramids in Egypt, the skinny towers stretching towards the sky in Italian hill towns, and the gothic cathedrals of France. While these types of buildings may look very different from each other, they all have one thing in __common/conclusion/contrast/addition__ . They were built with masonry or stone walls supporting most of the weight (so-called load-bearing walls), including that of the floors, the people, and everything the rooms contained. Because of this, the height of these buildings was limited by how massive and heavy they had to be at the base. Two __developments/metropolises/contributions/leverages__ in the 19th century paved the way for a whole new type of building: the skyscraper. The first was the development of a safe elevator. Primitive elevators of various designs had been used for centuries, and starting in the mid 19th century, steam-operated elevators were used to move materials in factories, mines, and warehouses. But these elevators were not __considered/manipulated/provisioned/stipulated__ safe for people; if the cable broke, they would plummet to the bottom of the elevator shaft.
items.fullText: The desire to build big is nothing new. Big buildings have been used to show off power and wealth; to honor leaders or religious beliefs; to stretch the limits of what's possible; and even as simple competition among owners, families, architects, and builders. Some of the most dramatic buildings of the past include the pyramids in Egypt, the skinny towers stretching towards the sky in Italian hill towns, and the gothic cathedrals of France. While these types of buildings may look very different from each other, they all have one thing in common . They were built with masonry or stone walls supporting most of the weight (so-called load-bearing walls), including that of the floors, the people, and everything the rooms contained. Because of this, the height of these buildings was limited by how massive and heavy they had to be at the base. Two developments in the 19th century paved the way for a whole new type of building: the skyscraper. The first was the development of a safe elevator. Primitive elevators of various designs had been used for centuries, and starting in the mid 19th century, steam-operated elevators were used to move materials in factories, mines, and warehouses. items.beginnerText: People have always wanted to build big things. Big buildings show power and money. They honor leaders or religions. They test what is possible. Sometimes, they are just a contest between owners, families, builders, and architects. Some amazing old buildings are the pyramids in Egypt and tall towers in Italy. Also, the gothic churches in France are very impressive. These buildings look different. But they have something in common. They used stone walls to hold the weight (load-bearing walls). This included the floors, people, and everything inside. So, these buildings could not be too tall. They would need very big, heavy bases. In the 1800s, two things helped create a new kind of building: the skyscraper. First, someone made a safe elevator. Old elevators were used for a long time. items.intermediateText: The ambition to construct large buildings is not a recent phenomenon. Throughout history, grand structures have served to display power and wealth, to commemorate influential figures or religious doctrines, to push the boundaries of architectural possibilities, and even to foster competition among owners, families, architects, and builders. Notable examples from the past include the Egyptian pyramids, the slender towers reaching skyward in Italian hill towns, and the gothic cathedrals of France. Although these buildings appear quite different, they share a key characteristic. Their construction relied on masonry or stone walls to bear the majority of the weight (known as load-bearing walls), encompassing the floors, occupants, and contents of the rooms. Consequently, the height of these buildings was restricted by the immense size and weight required at their base. However, two advancements in the 19th century facilitated the emergence of a novel building type: the skyscraper. The first was the invention of a secure elevator. While basic elevators had existed for centuries, steam-powered elevators began to be used in the mid-1800s to transport materials in industrial settings like factories, mines, and warehouses. Nevertheless, these early elevators were deemed unsafe for passengers, as a broken cable would cause them to fall rapidly to the bottom of the shaft.

items.fullText: Look at the recent "Most Respected Companies" survey by the Financial Times. Who are the most respected companies and business leaders at the current time? items.title: #55 Below-ground Organisms

items.fullText: If you want to find unique diversity and if you want to find a wide range of different below-ground organisms, you don't have to travel around the world. You can walk across Central Park. That statement comes from Noah Fierer, an ecology and evolutionary biology professor at the University of Colorado, Boulder. He's also a coauthor of a study that uncovered the surprisingly large diversity of subterranean microbial life at the 843-acre green rectangle in the heart of Manhattan. The research is in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B. Investigators looked at 596 separate soil samples from the park and found thousands of different types of microbes . They also compared those microbes with those living in 52 other soil samples taken from all around the planet. The park had organisms that also exist in deserts, frozen tundra, forests, rainforests and prairies. Antarctica was the only area that had microbes that did not overlap with those found in Central Park. And only a small percentage of the park's microbes were found to be already listed in databases. The variety of microbes probably reflects a diversity of soil conditions within the park. Seems that New York is a melting pot for people above the surface. And for microbes beneath it.
items.beginnerText: You don't need to travel the world to see many types of tiny living things. You can just walk in Central Park. Noah Fierer says this. He teaches about ecology and biology at the University of Colorado, Boulder. He helped write a study. The study found many different tiny living things in the soil of Central Park. Central Park is a big green space in New York City. The study is in a journal called the Proceedings of the Royal Society B. Scientists looked at 596 soil samples from the park. They found thousands of types of microbes (very small living things). They compared these microbes to microbes from 52 other places on Earth. Central Park had microbes that also live in deserts, cold areas, forests, and rainforests. Only Antarctica had microbes not found in Central Park. Most of the park's microbes were new to science. The different microbes are there because the soil in the park is different in many places. New York is a mix of people above the ground. It is also a mix of microbes below the ground.
items.intermediateText: You don't have to travel the globe to discover unique diversity and a wide variety of below-ground organisms. Instead, you can simply explore Central Park. This statement is according to Noah Fierer, a professor of ecology and evolutionary biology at the University of Colorado, Boulder. Fierer is also a coauthor of a study that revealed a surprisingly large diversity of subterranean microbial life within Central Park, the 843-acre green space in Manhattan. The research appears in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B. Researchers examined 596 soil samples from the park and identified thousands of different types of microbes (very small organisms). These microbes were then compared to those found in 52 other soil samples taken from around the world. The park contained organisms that are also present in diverse environments such as deserts, frozen tundra, forests, rainforests, and prairies. Only Antarctica had microbes that did not overlap with those found in Central Park. Furthermore, only a small percentage of the park's microbes were already listed in databases. The variety of microbes likely reflects the diverse soil conditions within the park. It seems New York is a melting pot not only for people above the surface but also for microbes beneath it.

items.title: #56 Agrarian Parties
items.answerText: Agrarian parties are political parties chiefly representing the interests of peasants or, more broadly, the rural sector of society. The extent to which they are important, or __whether/where/why/how/what__ they even exist, depends mainly on two factors. One, obviously, is the size of an identifiable peasantry, or the size of the rural relative __to/from/of/on/with__ the urban population. The other is a matter of social integration: __for/as/in/to/by__ agrarian parties to be important, the representation of countryside or peasantry must not be integrated with the other major sections of society. __However/Thus/Meanwhile/Moreover/Nevertheless__ , a country might possess a sizable rural population, but have an economic system in which the interests of the voters were predominantly related to their incomes, __rather/higher/lower/other/fewer__ than their occupations or location; and in such a country the political system would be unlikely to include an important agrarian party.
items.fullText: Agrarian parties are political parties chiefly representing the interests of peasants or, more broadly, the rural sector of society. The extent to which they are important, or whether they even exist, depends mainly on two factors. One, obviously, is the size of an identifiable peasantry, or the size of the rural relative to the urban population. The other is a matter of social integration: for agrarian parties to be important, the representation of countryside or peasantry must not be integrated with the other major sections of society. However , a country might possess a sizable rural population, but have an economic system in which the interests of the voters were predominantly related to their incomes, rather than their occupations or location; and in such a country the political system would be unlikely to include an important agrarian party.
items.beginnerText: Agrarian parties are political groups. They mainly represent farmers or people in the countryside. How important they are depends on two things. First, it depends on how many farmers there are. It also depends on how many people live in the countryside compared to cities. Second, these parties are important if farmers are not part of other big groups in society. But, a country might have many people in the countryside. However, their money might matter more than their jobs or where they live. Then, the country probably will not have an important agrarian party.
items.intermediateText: Agrarian parties are political parties that mainly represent the interests of farmers, or more generally, people in rural areas. Their importance depends on two main factors. First, it depends on the size of the farming population, or the size of the rural population compared to the urban population. Second, it depends on social integration. Agrarian parties are important if the concerns of rural people are not already represented within other major parts of society. However, even if a country has a large rural population, its economic system might focus more on people's incomes than their jobs or locations. In that case, the political system is unlikely to have a significant agrarian party.

items.title: #57 Retirement
items.answerText: For a start, we need to change our __concept/contempt/confrontation/conclusion__ of 'retirement', and we need to change mind-sets arising from earlier government policy which, in the face of high unemployment levels, encouraged mature workers to take early retirement. Today, government encourages them to __delay/replay/relay/drag__ their retirement. We now need to think of retirement as a phased process, where mature age workers __gradually/radically/disruptively/abruptly__ reduce their hours, and where they have considerable flexibility in how they combine their work and non work time. We also need to recognise the broader change that is occurring in how people work, learn, and live. Increasingly we are moving away from a linear relationship between education, training, work, and retirement, as people move in and out of jobs, careers, caregiving, study, and leisure. Employers of choice remove the __barriers/hinges/nexus/bans__ between the different segments of people's lives, by creating flexible conditions of work and a range of leave entitlements. They take an individualized approach to workforce planning and development so that the needs of employers and employees can be met __simultaneously/condescendingly/hypocritically/spontaneously__ .
items.fullText: For a start, we need to change our concept of 'retirement', and we need to change mind-sets arising from earlier government policy which, in the face of high unemployment levels, encouraged mature workers to take early retirement. Today, government encourages them to delay their retirement. We now need to think of retirement as a phased process, where mature age workers gradually reduce their hours, and where they have considerable flexibility in how they combine their work and non work time. We also need to recognise the broader change that is occurring in how people work, learn, and live. Increasingly we are moving away from a linear relationship between education, training, work, and retirement, as people move in and out of jobs, careers, caregiving, study, and leisure. Employers of choice remove the barriers between the different segments of people's lives, by creating flexible conditions of work and a range of leave entitlements. They take an individualized approach to workforce planning and development so that the needs of employers and employees can be met simultaneously .
items.beginnerText: First, we must change how we think about 'retirement'. We also need to change our ideas about it. Past government plans told older workers to retire early because there were not enough jobs. Now, the government wants them to retire later. We should now see retirement as a slow change. Older workers can work fewer hours little by little. They can choose how to mix their work and free time. Also, people now work, learn, and live in new ways. We are moving away from the old idea where education, work, and retirement always follow each other. People now change jobs, careers, take care of family, study, and enjoy free time. Good employers make it easier to balance work and life. They offer flexible work and different types of time off. They plan for each worker's needs. This helps both the company and the workers.
items.intermediateText: To begin, we must update our understanding of 'retirement'. We also need to shift the mindsets that came from older government policies. These policies encouraged older workers to retire early due to high unemployment. Now, the government encourages them to postpone retirement. We should now view retirement as a gradual process. Older workers can slowly decrease their working hours. They should also have the freedom to balance their work and personal time. Furthermore, we must acknowledge the wider changes in how people work, learn, and live. We are increasingly moving away from a simple, direct path of education, training, work, and retirement. People now often switch between jobs, careers, caregiving, education, and leisure. The best employers remove obstacles between different parts of people’s lives. They do this by offering flexible work arrangements and various leave options. They use a personalized method for planning and developing their workforce. These are called free electrons. Free electrons can move between atoms. This movement is called electron flow. Electricity is when electrons move from one atom to another. items.intermediateText: Electrons orbiting closest to the nucleus experience a strong attraction and are known as bound electrons. In contrast, electrons farther from the nucleus can be forced out of their orbits; these are termed free electrons. Free electrons are capable of moving from one atom to another, a process referred to as electron flow. Electricity, essentially, is the movement of electrons between atoms. For electron movement to occur, a condition of imbalance is required. Typically, a normal atom maintains balance between its positively charged nucleus and negatively charged electrons, which keeps them in orbit. However, if an atom loses electrons, it acquires a positive charge and seeks to attract more electrons to restore its balance. A conductor is a material that facilitates electron flow, thus conducting electricity. Effective conductors consist of atoms that readily release free electrons. Furthermore, the proximity of atoms to each other is crucial, ensuring that the orbits of free electrons overlap. For example, ignition systems utilize copper and aluminum wires to conduct electricity, allowing for efficient electron flow.

He observed that individuals differ in their inherited traits and that selection acts on such differences, leading to evolutionary change. Although Darwin realized that variation in heritable traits is a prerequisite for evolution , he did not know precisely how organisms pass heritable traits to their offspring. Just a few years after Darwin published The Origin of Species, Gregor Mendel wrote a groundbreaking paper on inheritance in pea plants. In that paper, Mendel proposed a model of inheritance in which organisms transmit discrete heritable units (now called genes) to their offspring. Darwin knew that changes in traits are needed for evolution. But he did not know how living things pass traits to their young. Soon after Darwin's book, Gregor Mendel wrote an important paper. items.intermediateText: In The Origin of Species, Darwin presented considerable evidence supporting the evolution of life on Earth over time. He suggested natural selection as the main process driving this change. Darwin noticed that individuals have different inherited traits. Selection acts upon these differences, resulting in evolutionary change. Although Darwin understood that variation in heritable traits is essential for evolution, he did not know how organisms pass these traits to their offspring. Shortly after Darwin published The Origin of Species, Gregor Mendel wrote an important paper about inheritance in pea plants. In this paper, Mendel proposed that organisms pass on separate units of heredity (now known as genes) to their offspring. While Darwin was unaware of genes, Mendel's work paved the way for understanding the genetic variations that underlie evolution.

These large, flightless birds have small, feathered forelimbs. Scientists used to think these were only for display or to control their body temperature. Further research could provide a more accurate picture of dinosaur movement in their prehistoric environment.

They considered substances like walnut oil as potentially pure as silver, even though modern scientists would classify one as heterogeneous (mixed composition) and the other as homogeneous (uniform composition). Consequently, without knowledge of atomic structures, how could one differentiate between elements and compounds?

Enhanced bitter sensing results in a stronger response. Consequently, researchers at the Monell Chemical Senses Center are working on developing a universal taste test. This test would provide a standardized way to measure how well we perceive flavors, because a key to better health might depend on our sense of taste.

items.title: #118 Musical Experiences

items.fullText: The general perception is that children are surrounded by a variety of musical experiences. There are often fewer and fewer opportunities for children to actively engage in music making themselves. They are inundated with music emitting from a wide array of electronic devices, toys, and computers offering a limitless number of musical selections. However, much of the music in children's lives is 'unchosen', in other words they are passive recipients in much of the music in their lives, and not actively engaged in its selection. They experience background music in computer games, cartoons, TV shows, films, on iPads, radios, and ringtones. They listen to music choices of their parents or siblings, and even the schools they attend often play music before the school day begins or in classrooms while students are working. Studies are being conducted on the effects of the ubiquitous pre-recorded music they encounter and whether or not it is intruding on their desire to make their own music or interact with each other on the playground.
items.beginnerText: Many people think that kids have lots of musical experiences. But kids have fewer chances to make music themselves. They hear music from many things like phones, toys, and computers. There are endless songs to pick from. But much of this music is 'unchosen.' This means kids don't pick the music. They just listen. They hear music in games, cartoons, shows, movies, iPads, radios, and ringtones. They listen to what their parents or siblings like. Schools also play music before class or when kids are working. Some studies look at how this constant music affects kids. They want to know if it stops kids from wanting to make their own music or play with others.
items.intermediateText: Generally, people believe that children are exposed to many kinds of music. However, children now have fewer chances to actively make music themselves. They are surrounded by music from many electronic devices, toys, and computers that offer many choices. Yet, much of the music in children's lives is 'unchosen.' This means they often passively receive music instead of actively choosing it. They hear background music in games, cartoons, TV, movies, iPads, radios, and ringtones. Also, they listen to music chosen by their parents or siblings. Even schools often play music before the day starts or while students work. items.title: #133 Gorongosa
items.answerText: Gorongosa, which was a jewel of Southern Africa…had great populations of lions, elephants, hippos, buffalo, etcetera. Absolutely decimated. So if you went there in the early part of the last decade, in the early 2000s, you might drive for five or six hours and see one warthog, one baboon, maybe. Biologist Sean B. Carroll, of the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and the University of Wisconsin-Madison. He spoke March 15th in the Great Hall of the Cooper Union here in New York City about his latest book The Serengeti Rules: The Quest to Discovery How Life Works, and Why It Matters. Gorongosa National Park was ravaged during the Mozambique war for independence from Portugal and then the civil war that followed. "And a __philanthropist/passion/solstice/ballast__ , Greg Carr…was looking for a project to really sink his teeth into and to work on human __development/negligence/prevalence/malevolence__ , became also really interested in conservation, learned about Mozambique…and in 2004 committed a sizeable fortune to helping to restore Gorongosa in partnership with the Mozambique __government/parliament/semanticist/journalist__ . And in 2004 surveys showed there were fewer than one __thousand/deflowered/embowered/roundest__ large animals in the entire park, and this is a massive place. So that's all antelope and elephants, all combined, fewer than a thousand of all types combined. "And I was there last summer as the new survey came in. A decade later: 72,000 large animals. Dramatic change. I'm looking at elephant herds with lots of youngsters. I'm looking at hippos, groups of hippos…. "So the point is this: the habitat was all there. The large animals had been shot, poached, used for food, whatever, but the habitat was still there and still __productive/assertive/incidental/compulsive__ . And once these very small remnant populations had that pressure taken off them, they've just been booming. And so a place that, I think it's the one place on Earth I know that's been the most decimated and has seen the greatest __recovery/efficacy/golly/stumpy__ … "So there's a lot of stories of good management and of recovery, and recovery on that really rapid time frame. And I think that's where I find hope. And when I said that Greg Carr committed a sizeable amount of money, I'm just gonna tell you exactly what that is, he spent about the same amount of money inside the park as outside the park, on human development, health care, education, etcetera, for Mozambicans, economic development. But in the park it's about a $3-million-a-year budget. Three million bucks a year to bring back a vast African wilderness. In the time of my explanation alone, how much did we just blow on like the worst ideas that possibly came out of Washington? "My optimism is that it can be cheaper than you think, it's faster than you think—and it's not a luxury. I'm not just talking about making pretty places prettier. It's making everything functional. And this, I think, is why I took certain examples in the book about from agriculture and fisheries and things like that, because we need our systems to be productive. There's 7.4 billion of us, and if we're not managing them in a productive way, that's gonna show up in some pretty horrible ways."

items.beginnerText: Gorongosa was a beautiful place in Southern Africa. It had many lions, elephants, hippos, and buffalo. But the animals were almost all gone. If you went there in the early 2000s, you might drive for hours. You might only see one warthog or baboon. Sean B. Carroll is a biologist. He works at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and the University of Wisconsin-Madison. On March 15th, he talked about his new book. The book is called The Serengeti Rules: The Quest to Discovery How Life Works, and Why It Matters. He spoke in New York City. Gorongosa National Park was damaged in wars. First, there was a war for independence from Portugal. Then, there was a civil war. Greg Carr is a philanthropist (a person who gives money to help others). He wanted to find a project to work on. He wanted to help people and nature. He learned about Mozambique. In 2004, he gave a lot of money to help Gorongosa. He worked with the Mozambique government. In 2004, there were less than one thousand big animals in the park. The park is very big. There were antelope and elephants. There were less than one thousand of all types of animals. Last summer, I was there when they did a new survey. Ten years later, there were 72,000 big animals. This was a big change. I saw elephant herds with baby elephants. I saw groups of hippos. The habitat was still there. The animals had been shot or used for food. But the habitat was still good. When the pressure was taken off the animals, they started to grow in numbers. This place was almost destroyed. But it has recovered the most. There are many stories of good management and recovery. The recovery happened quickly. This gives me hope. Greg Carr spent a lot of money. He spent about the same amount of money inside the park and outside the park. He spent money on health care, education, and economic development for Mozambicans. The park's budget is about $3 million a year. Three million dollars a year can bring back a big African wilderness. We spend much more money on bad ideas in Washington. I am optimistic. It can be cheaper and faster than you think. It is important to protect nature. It is not just about making places pretty. It is about making them work well. That is why I used examples from agriculture and fisheries in my book. We need our systems to be productive. There are 7.4 billion people. If we do not manage our systems well, there will be problems.
items.intermediateText: Gorongosa, once a jewel of Southern Africa, had abundant populations of lions, elephants, hippos, and buffalo. However, the populations were almost completely decimated. In the early 2000s, a visitor might drive for five or six hours and only see a warthog or a baboon. Biologist Sean B. Carroll, from the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and the University of Wisconsin-Madison, spoke on March 15th in New York City. He discussed his latest book, The Serengeti Rules: The Quest to Discovery How Life Works, and Why It Matters. Gorongosa National Park suffered greatly during the Mozambique war for independence from Portugal and the subsequent civil war. Greg Carr, a philanthropist, sought a project to dedicate himself to, focusing on human development. He also became interested in conservation and learned about Mozambique. In 2004, he invested a significant amount of money to help restore Gorongosa in partnership with the Mozambique government. Surveys in 2004 indicated that there were fewer than one thousand large animals in the entire park, which is a very large area. This included all antelope and elephants. There were less than a thousand animals of all types combined. The speaker recounted visiting the park the previous summer when a new survey was completed. A decade later, there were 72,000 large animals, a dramatic change. He observed elephant herds with many young animals and groups of hippos. The key point is that the habitat remained intact. Although the large animals had been shot, poached, or used for food, the habitat was still productive. Once the pressure on the small remaining populations was reduced, they thrived. This place, which was among the most devastated on Earth, has seen a remarkable recovery. There are many stories of effective management and rapid recovery. This is a source of hope. Greg Carr's financial commitment involved spending roughly the same amount of money inside the park as outside the park. The funds supported human development, health care, education, and economic development for Mozambicans. The park's budget is approximately $3 million per year. This relatively modest sum is helping to restore a vast African wilderness. Comparatively, much more is spent on ineffective projects elsewhere. The speaker expressed optimism that conservation can be more affordable and faster than commonly believed. It is not merely a luxury to make places aesthetically pleasing, but about ensuring that ecosystems function effectively. This is why he included examples from agriculture and fisheries in his book, emphasizing the need for productive systems to support the world's 7.4 billion people. Ineffectively managing these systems will lead to dire consequences.

items.beginnerText: On November 24, 1974, Donald Johanson found Lucy in Ethiopia. He is a paleoanthropologist (someone who studies old human bones). Many people think Lucy is the most famous human ancestor fossil. Last month, Johanson spoke about seeing Lucy for the first time at a meeting. He said, "In 1974, I was with Tom Gray, a student. We walked back to our car to go back to camp. We wanted to swim in the river with crocodiles and have lunch. I always look at the ground. I find coins easily! You often find what you look for. A year before, a geologist looked for rocks near the skeleton. He left footprints. I looked for bones. I found a small piece of elbow. It helps us move our arm. I knew it was from a human ancestor because I studied bones and anatomy." Johanson continued, "I looked up and saw more pieces. We dug for two weeks. We found about 40 percent of the skeleton (not counting hands and feet). This was important because it was over three million years old. Before this, all fossils older than three million years were very small. We didn't know it was a new kind of human until 1978. We named it Australopithecus afarensis." Her blog is called The Fossil That Revolutionized the Search for Human Origins: A Q&A with Lucy Discoverer Donald Johanson.

I always look at the ground carefully. It’s like you find what you're looking for. A year before the discovery, a geologist had left footprints near the skeleton while searching for rocks. I was looking for bones. I found a small piece of an elbow, which allows us to bend our arm. From my studies of osteology (the study of bones) and comparative anatomy, I knew it was from a human ancestor." He added, "Looking up the slope, I saw more fragments eroding. Before this, all fossils older than three million years were very small. We didn't realize it was a new species until we published the name Australopithecus afarensis in 1978." For more information, see the blog post on our website by Scientific American's Kate Wong, who co-authored the book Lucy's Legacy with Johanson. Kate's blog is titled The Fossil That Revolutionized the Search for Human Origins: A Q&A with Lucy Discoverer Donald Johanson.
