items.fullText: I do not think I am twisting the usual meaning of drama if I define it as a presentation before spectators by performers who take on roles and who interact with each other to further a story or a text intended for such presentations. This is intended as a working definition simple enough to be recalled easily. Indeed, it is so simple that I should point out that it makes one or two distinctions that are perhaps not immediately obvious. First, to say that performers "take on roles" leaves open the possibility that they are not within the roles to other performances as such alternative phrases as "performers in character" or "characters represented by actors" do not. To say that the performers "interact with each other" might seem unnecessary , but is in fact important, for in traditional societies there are many performances in which different characters appear successively and simultaneously but, nevertheless , do not interact. And I say "to further a story" because a progression of the story may not provide the structure of the performance.
items.beginnerText: I want to define drama. I think of it as a show for people to watch. In the show, actors play roles. They talk to each other to help tell a story. Or they act out a text made for shows. This is a simple definition that is easy to remember. It is so simple that it makes some things clear that you might not notice at first. First, when actors "take on roles," it means they might not always be fully in those roles. This is different from saying "performers in character." Second, saying actors "interact with each other" is important. In some cultures, characters appear one after another or at the same time. But they do not talk to each other. Also, I say "to help tell a story" because the order of events in the story might not be how the show is set up.
items.intermediateText: I believe my definition of drama aligns with its common understanding: a presentation for an audience, featuring performers who embody roles and engage with one another to advance a narrative or a script designed for such presentations. This definition is meant to be practical and easily remembered. It is simple, yet it highlights some distinctions that might not be immediately apparent. Firstly, stating that performers "take on roles" suggests that they may not be entirely confined to those roles, unlike alternative expressions such as "performers in character" or "characters represented by actors." Secondly, specifying that the performers "interact with each other" is crucial because, in many traditional societies, performances involve various characters appearing in sequence or concurrently, yet without interacting. Finally, the phrase "to further a story" is used because the story's progression might not dictate the performance's structure.

items.fullText: The study of objects constitutes a relatively new field of academic enquiry, commonly referred to as material culture studies. Students of material culture seek to understand societies, both past and present, through careful study and observation of the physical or material objects generated by those societies. The source material for study is exceptionally wide, including not just human-made artefacts but also natural objects and even preserved body parts (as you saw in the film 'Encountering a body'). items.fullText: People have been buzzing this week about a study from Johns Hopkins University on mosquitoes, genetically engineered to be resistant to malaria. The idea is to introduce the modified insects into an area affected by the disease and have them completely replace the native population. If the mosquitoes can't get infected, the logic goes, then the people they bite won't either. But to make that scheme work, transgenic mosquitoes need to outcompete the locals. So scientists at Johns Hopkins tested their ability to do this, by allowing equal numbers of resistant and non-resistant mosquitoes to feed on the blood of malaria-infected mice. After nine generations, the transgenic mosquitoes made up 70 percent of the population, meaning they survived better and laid more eggs than the ordinary ones. Winning a head-to-head contest in the lab, though, doesn't mean the same thing will happen out in the field. There are a lot of mosquitoes out there, and elbowing them out won't be easy. It is nonetheless a stunning number, which refutes the claim by some environmentalists that permanent economic growth is fundamentally incompatible with finite physical resources.
items.beginnerText: The most interesting changes are not just about fossil fuels. The energy intensity of the world economy is dropping. Energy intensity means how much energy we need to make one dollar. It is going down by about 2 percent each year. This means the economy can grow by 2 percent without using more energy from fossil fuels. But this is not enough to stop climate change. We need the economy to grow even more. Still, this 2 percent drop is amazing. Some people who care about the environment say that the economy cannot grow forever because we have limited resources. But this number shows they may be wrong.

Energy intensity refers to the amount of energy needed to generate one dollar of economic output. This metric is falling by approximately 2 percent annually. Consequently, even if the proportion of fossil-based versus fossil-free energy sources remains constant, the world could experience 2 percent annual economic growth without a corresponding increase in carbon emissions. While this alone is insufficient to combat climate change, and further economic growth is necessary, this decrease is still significant. It challenges the assertion by some environmentalists that continuous economic growth is fundamentally unsustainable given the planet's finite resources.

At night, they saw the moon. Each night, the moon seemed to grow or shrink a bit. Sometimes, it did not appear at all. At night, tiny lights dotted the sky. People called these lights stars. They thought each star had a reason for being there. They believed they could learn the universe's secrets by studying the stars. Some stars seemed to wander. items.intermediateText: From the earliest civilizations, humans have been curious about the world, its creation, and its eventual end. In ancient times, the sun was observed making its daily journey across the sky, while the moon appeared at night. The moon's phases changed nightly, sometimes disappearing completely. The night sky was filled with countless points of light, which were named stars. People believed that each star had a unique purpose and that studying them could reveal the universe's secrets. Furthermore, some stars, known as planets, appeared to wander, changing their positions relative to other stars each night. It took centuries, indeed millennia, to understand the true nature of these wandering stars, develop a model of the world that accounted for them, and accurately predict their movements in the sky.

items.fullText: At the end of the colonial era, as many new nations gained independence, relative levels of economic development became an important criterion by which to distinguish between countries. The former colonial powers and wealthier parts of the world generally became known as advanced industrial, or developed countries, while former colonies and poorer nations became known as less developed, or more positively, developing countries. Critics of the uneven distribution of wealth across the globe highlighted the role which wealth creation in some places had played in impoverishing poorer nations and, rather, described them as actively underdeveloped. items.beginnerText: Many new countries became free after the colonial era. Then, how rich a country was became a key way to compare them. Richer countries were called “developed.” Poorer countries were called “developing.” Some people said that rich countries made poor countries poorer. items.intermediateText: As the colonial era ended and many nations became independent, economic development became a key way to compare countries. Former colonial powers and richer nations were often called “developed countries.” Former colonies and poorer nations were called “developing countries.” However, some critics argued that the wealth of some countries contributed to the impoverishment of others, describing the latter as “underdeveloped.” The question of whether economic changes truly develop countries or actually underdevelop them remains important, as illustrated by the ongoing debate over sweatshops.

This is vital in today's rapidly changing world, not just here in Hong Kong, but especially in Southeast Asia which holds the world's most diverse marine habitats. SWIMS is playing a major role in trying to measure and conserve these important resources, both within Hong Kong but also, together with its regional collaborators, in Southeast Asia." said Professor Gray A. Williams, the study leader and Director of HKU SWIMS. However, the vast array of marine life in Hong Kong has not yet received enough conservation. Currently, less than 2% of Hong Kong's marine area is protected as marine parks or reserves, compared to about 40% of its land area. The Government has promised to create more marine parks in the coming years. The Brothers Marine Park in northern Lantau will open soon, increasing Hong Kong's total protected marine area to over 2%. The research team supports the new marine park. They also urge the Hong Kong government to work towards the global target of protecting at least 10% of marine areas by 2020, as set by the United Nation's Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD).

items.title: #186 Welfare Morality

items.fullText: The morality of the welfare state depends on contribution and responsibility. Since some people don't contribute and many are irresponsible, the choices of those who do contribute and are responsible are either to tolerate the free riders, refuse to pay for the effects of their irresponsibility or trust the state to educate them. Hence the government campaigns against smoking, alcoholism, obesity and gas guzzling ‐ the first two solidly in place, the other two ramping up. But the British state now goes further: it acts in favor of sexual and racial minorities. In the case of gay men and women this means progressively removing the legal disadvantages under which they have lived, and ensuring that society as a whole observes the new order.
items.beginnerText: If people want help from the government, they should work hard and be responsible. Some people don't work, and some are not responsible. Then, people who work hard can do a few things. They can accept those who don't work. Or, they can refuse to pay for the problems of those who are not responsible. Or, they can trust the government to teach them to be better. So, the government fights things like smoking and drinking too much. They also fight being too fat and using too much gas. items.intermediateText: The ethical basis of the welfare state relies on people contributing and acting responsibly. Because some individuals do not contribute, and many act irresponsibly, those who do contribute and are responsible face a choice. They can either accept those who take advantage (free riders), refuse to cover the costs of others' irresponsibility, or rely on the government to educate them. Consequently, the government has campaigns against smoking, alcoholism, obesity, and excessive gas usage. The first two are well-established, and the latter two are growing. However, the British government is now extending its reach. It is now acting to support sexual and racial minorities. For gay men and women, this involves gradually eliminating the legal disadvantages they have faced. It also means ensuring that society as a whole respects the new, more equitable standards.

items.fullText: Two decades ago, Kashmiri houseboat-owners rubbed their hands every spring at the prospect of the annual influx of tourists . From May to October, the hyacinth-choked waters of Dal Lake saw flotillas of vividly painted Shikaras carrying Indian families, boho westerners, young travellers and wide-eyed Japanese. items.intermediateText: Two decades ago, Kashmiri houseboat owners looked forward to the yearly arrival of tourists. Every spring, they anticipated a busy season. From May to October, Dal Lake's waters, thick with hyacinth, were filled with Shikaras (small boats) carrying various tourists, including Indian families and Western travelers. The lake became polluted, and the houseboats deteriorated. Foreigners who traveled there faced risks, as demonstrated in 1995 when five young Europeans were kidnapped and murdered.

items.title: #188 Migrating Birds

items.fullText: For birdwatchers in southern New Mexico, September can be highly entertaining. Good numbers of many diverse species are on the move during this time, traveling southward from northern breeding grounds to places they will spend the winter, and there's always a chance that some rare or unusual bird will turn up. Key to the flow of migrating birds through the area is our geography. Birds crossing over the southwest deserts tend to follow north-south watercourses like the Rio Grande and/or corridors of relatively green vegetation , whether that be cottonwoods and willows lining the valleys or the coniferous forests of the higher mountains. Shorebirds, gulls, ducks and other birds that are closely associated with water typically follow the river southward, unless a desert playa along the way happens to catch their eye and divert them. Migrating land birds, on the other hand, are looking for places to stop and rest on the southward journey, where they can feed on seeds, berries or insects to refuel for the next leg of their trip. Heading south out of Albuquerque, where the surrounding high mountains and lush, wide cottonwood bosques offer an abundance of habitat, they reach our area and are funneled into a relatively narrow sliver of foraging choices.
items.beginnerText: If you like birdwatching, southern New Mexico in September is fun. Many kinds of birds move south then. They fly from the north to warmer places for the winter. Sometimes, you can see a rare bird. The area's geography is important for these birds. Birds flying over the desert often follow rivers, like the Rio Grande. Or, they fly where there are green plants. This could be trees near rivers or forests in the mountains. Water birds like ducks usually follow the river south. But they might stop at a desert playa (a dry lakebed). Land birds look for places to rest on their trip. They eat seeds, berries, or bugs to get energy. When they fly south from Albuquerque, there are many mountains and trees. When the birds get to our area, there are fewer places for them to find food.
items.intermediateText: September is an entertaining month for birdwatchers in southern New Mexico. Many different bird species migrate during this time. They travel south from their northern breeding areas to their winter homes. There is also a chance to see rare or unusual birds. The geography of the area is key to understanding bird migration patterns. Birds flying across the southwest deserts often follow north-south watercourses, such as the Rio Grande. Alternatively, they use corridors of green vegetation, like cottonwoods and willows in valleys, or coniferous forests in the mountains. Shorebirds, gulls, and ducks often follow the river south. However, they might be diverted by a desert playa (a shallow, dry lakebed). On the other hand, migrating land birds look for places to rest and refuel. They eat seeds, berries, or insects to prepare for the next part of their journey. As they head south from Albuquerque, the birds leave behind the high mountains and cottonwood forests that offer plenty of habitats. Consequently, when they reach our area, they find themselves in a narrow region with limited foraging options.

They also cling to walls in a similar manner to geckos, utilizing small, hairy foot pads that enable them to stick to surfaces as if they were wearing Velcro socks. This was discovered when the physicists measured the force required to push a single mosquito leg into a cup of water. The reason the legs are so hydrophobic is that they are covered with tiny, featherlike scales, which in turn are covered by even smaller ribbing. Therefore, the next time you swat a mosquito, remember that you have just struck a marvel of nature.

items.title: #228 Manga
items.answerText: If Japan's rise to economic superpower dominated U.S. academic discussions in the 1980s, the last 15 years or so have been __marked/dedicated/made/inspired__ by an intense fascination, both in academic and popular discourse, with the country's perceived increase in global cultural influence. As Pokémon and Hello Kitty invaded U.S. TV screens and supermarket aisles at a time when, paradoxically, Japanese economic influence was on the decline, U.S. scholars started to point to the emergence of a new kind of Japanese superpower. The discussion shifted from Japan's Gross National Product to its "Gross National Cool". The characters in Japanese animated cartoon series and in the related genre of manga (Japanese-style comic books or graphic novels), along with their video game cousins, came to symbolize a new order in millennial capitalism __characterized/pocessed/opposed/tangled__ by a decline in U.S. cultural hegemony and the fragmentation of global powers. Thus, Japanese animation provides a logical starting point to an analysis aimed at decentralizing the role of the United States as the world’s most significant global cultural producer. This chapter will demonstrate, however, that while intending to point to Japan's growing influence and to a __concomitant/discrete/proportional/legitimate__ relative decline in U.S. power, the academic and popular discourse about Japanese animation's "global" popularity has paradoxically resulted in the re-centralizing of the United States as both a global cultural producer and a consumer of globalized cultural forms. Turning a translocal lens to the genre's transnational spread, this chapter illustrates the multiple ways in which this discourse is problematic. Throughout the chapter, the names of a few scholars will frequently reappear. These scholars are most assertively critiqued here not because their work is particularly problematic but, __on the contrary/however/in addition/on the whole__ , because they have produced the most comprehensive and sophisticated studies of Japanese animation and/or comics. Their works have become seminal texts in the academic study of Japanese popular culture in general and have greatly contributed to our understanding of its influence in the U.S. context. The chapter's deconstruction of these scholars' characterization of global processes is offered in an effort to illustrate the productive potential of a more translocal approach. It does not invalidate their __otherwise/likewise/likely/unlikely__ positive contributions to the field of Japanese studies.

They heated the sample to about 3,800 degrees Fahrenheit and applied 9.5 million pounds of pressure per square inch. They observed that iron combined with oxygen to create rust, leaving behind carbon, which then transformed into diamond. What if they studied a planet in a solar system with even more carbon? According to their model, the carbon would combine with iron to form a steel core. This would leave a carbon-rich mantle full of diamond. It is still unknown if the Milky Way contains such diamond planets. However, these planets probably could not support life, because diamonds transfer heat easily. A planet made of diamond would therefore be very cold.

items.title: #268 Flower Color

A yellow flower, for example, may look somewhat blue from one angle and red from another. Scientists call this kind of color change iridescence. 'It's the same phenomenon that makes a rainbow appear in a soap bubble or on a CD,' says Beverley Glover. She studies plants at the University of Cambridge in England. items.fullText: In many areas of expertise ranging from music, dance, art and literature to sports, chess, mathematics, science and foreign-language acquisition, there is abundant evidence that young people differ from one another in their attainments and in the apparent ease with which they achieve them. Even within a family there may be marked differences. For example, a child who struggles at a musical instrument without much success may be overtaken by a younger sibling. It is widely believed that the likelihood of becoming exceptionally competent in certain fields depends on the presence or absence of inborn attributes variously labelled 'talents' or 'gifts' or less often 'natural aptitudes'. According to an informal British survey, more than three-quarters of music educators who decide which young people are to receive instruction believe that children cannot do well, unless they have special innate gifts (Davis 1994). The judgement that someone is talented is believed to help explain (as distinct from merely describing) that person's success. It is also widely believed that the innate talent that makes it possible for an individual to excel can be detected in early childhood.
items.beginnerText: In many areas like music, art, sports, and science, there is proof that young people are different. They have different skills and learn at different speeds. Even in the same family, kids can be very different. For example, one child might find a musical instrument hard, but their younger brother or sister might be better at it. Many people think that being very good at something depends on having natural 'talents' or 'gifts'. One British study says that more than three-quarters of music teachers think kids need special gifts to do well (Davis 1994). People think that saying someone is 'talented' helps explain why they are successful. Many also think you can see this natural talent in young children.
items.intermediateText: In many fields, such as music, dance, art, literature, sports, chess, mathematics, science, and learning languages, there is much evidence that young people differ in their achievements and how easily they reach them. Even within families, there can be clear differences. For instance, a child who struggles with a musical instrument may be surpassed by a younger sibling. It is widely thought that becoming very skilled in certain areas depends on having inborn qualities, often called 'talents', 'gifts', or 'natural aptitudes'. According to an informal British survey, over three-quarters of music teachers who choose which young people will get lessons think that children cannot succeed without special innate gifts (Davis 1994). Judging someone as talented is thought to explain their success, rather than just describe it. It is also widely believed that the innate talent that allows someone to excel can be seen in early childhood.

items.title: #299 Civil War

In particular I will refer to Robert Lee Hodge, who was made famous by Tony Horwitz's 1996 book, Confederates in the Attic, and who served as a kind of Virgil to the author on his journey through a Confederate Valhalla. More than 30 percent went with the choice of other. items.title: #322 Christmas Cards
items.answerText: A few years ago, a university professor tried a little experiment. He sent Christmas cards to a sample of perfect strangers. The great majority of those who returned a card never inquired __into/through/over/after__ the identity of the unknown professor. They received his holiday greeting card, and they automatically sent one in return. This study shows the action of one of the most powerful of the weapons of influence around us — the rule for __reciprocation/adjudication/advocation/verification__ . The rule says that we should try to repay, in kind, what another person has provided us. If a woman does us a favor, we should do her one in return; if a man sends us a birthday present, we should remember his birthday with a gift of our own; if a couple invites us to a party, we should be sure to invite them to one of ours.

These closely related families then seek out other families with similar behaviors. As Cantor states, "They tend to hang out or stay together with those who produce the same kinds of sounds." This means that whale groups are formed based on similar clicks. Whales that click in similar ways not only stay together but also copy each other's songs, known as codas. Therefore, whale clans develop their own dialects, which are a form of culture. These dialects are key to their social structure. Cantor and his team created a computer simulation of virtual whales over generations. They discovered that culture, rather than genetics or mother-daughter teaching, explains the development of clans and dialects in sperm whale societies. This research appears in the journal Nature Communications. Cantor clarifies that whale culture is not identical to human culture, which is more diverse, complex, and symbolic. However, he finds it fascinating that whales have their own type of culture. He suggests that a better understanding of whale culture might encourage humans to be more conservation-minded towards whales.

Sociologists make the point that going to a conference is only partly about the presentations; in reality it is about the coffee, the chat, the jokes, the friendships and contacts you can make. A final thought for banks or for anybody suggesting business interactions can be virtual . Apple was the first computer company to open its own stores. Face to face interactions matter for consumers but also for brands and businesses. This is a salutary lesson for banks that they should be closing branches. In the commercial world analog products exist when they add value and deliver something the digital world misses. Central banks need to consider carefully the balance of physical and digital.

items.title: #360 Social Ties
items.answerText: Many types of scientific evidence show that involvement in social relationships benefits health. The most striking evidence comes from prospective studies of mortality __across/off/beneath/on__ industrialized nations. These studies __consistently/impotently/competently/inadvertently__ show that individuals with the lowest level of involvement in social relationships are more likely to die than those with greater involvement. The risk of death among men and women with the fewest social ties was more than twice as high as the risk for adults with the most social ties. Social ties also reduce __mortality/mentality/morality/mutuality__ risk among adults with documented medical conditions. Among adults with coronary artery disease, the socially isolated had a risk of subsequent cardiac death 2.4 times greater than their more socially connected __peers/sneers/careers/pioneers__ . items.title: #361 Idea of Beauty
items.answerText: When we are very concerned about certain of our physical __features/gestures/components/pastures__ — a nose that is stubbornly a bit too large, eyes that are slightly too far apart, hair that is not as lustrous as it should be — we miss an overall point about our relationship to our appearance: how beautiful we feel has nothing to do with the __objective/reflective/conjunctive/subjective__ structure of our face or body. It isn’t what we look like that counts: it's how we feel inside. Our self-assessments are in the end solely __based on/called in/ruled out/summed up__ our relative degrees of self-love and self-contempt. There are people of ideal __proportions/distortions/apportions/abortions__ and exceptional beauty who cannot bear what they see in the mirror and others who can contemplate a less than svelte stomach or a no longer so supple kind of skin with indifference and defiant good humor. And at a tragic __extreme/humanity/feeling/supreme__ , there are heart-breakingly fine-looking people who starve themselves to ill-health.
items.fullText: When we are very concerned about certain of our physical features — a nose that is stubbornly a bit too large, eyes that are slightly too far apart, hair that is not as lustrous as it should be — we miss an overall point about our relationship to our appearance: how beautiful we feel has nothing to do with the objective structure of our face or body. Some very beautiful people hate what they see in the mirror. Other people are okay with their body, even if it is not perfect. Sadly, some very good-looking people starve themselves and become sick.

items.title: #363 Plants and Animals
items.answerText: From the earliest civilisations, plants and animals have been portrayed as a means of understanding and recording the potential uses, such as their economic and healing properties. From the first illustrated __catalogue/calculation/formation/figuration__ of medicinal plants, De Materia Medica by Dioscorides, in the first century through to the late fourteenth century the illustration of plants and animals changed very little. Woodcuts in instructional manuals and herbals were often repeatedly copied over the centuries, resulting in a loss of definition and accuracy so that they became little more than stylized decoration. With the growing __popularity/popular/singularity/resilience__ of copperplate engravings, the traditional use of woodcuts declined and the representation of plants and animals became more accurate. Then, with the __emergence/descent/havoc/omniscience__ of artists such as Albrecht Durer and Leonardo Da Vinci, naturalists such as Otto Brunfels, Leonhard Fuchs in botany and Conrad Gesner and Ulisse Aldrovandi in zoology, nature began to be depicted in a more realistic style. Individual living plants or animals __were observed/observed/observe/had observed__ directly and their likeness was rendered onto paper or vellum.

items.title: #365 Why Students Forget
items.answerText: Teachers have long known that rote memorization can lead to a __superficial/similar/comprehensive/solid__ grasp of material that is quickly forgotten. But new research in the field of neuroscience is starting to __shed/flow/stream/charge__ light on the ways that brains are wired to forget — highlighting the importance of strategies to retain knowledge and make learning stick. In a recent article published in the journal Neuron, neurobiologists Blake Richards and Paul Frankland challenge the __predominant/prevented/prehistoric/presidential__ view of memory, which holds that forgetting is a process of loss — the gradual washing away of critical information __despite/through/yet/provided__ our best efforts to retain it. According to Richards and Frankland, the goal of memory is not just to store information accurately but to ‘optimize decision-making’ in chaotic, quickly changing environments. In this model of cognition, forgetting is an evolutionary strategy, a __purposeful/grateful/distrustful/thoughtful__ process that runs in the background of memory, evaluating and discarding information that doesn’t promote the survival of the species.
items.fullText: Teachers have long known that rote memorization can lead to a superficial grasp of material that is quickly forgotten. But new research in the field of neuroscience is starting to shed light on the ways that brains are wired to forget — highlighting the importance of strategies to retain knowledge and make learning stick. They say that forgetting is not just losing information. They say memory is not just about storing information well. It is about making good choices in fast-changing situations. In a recent article in the journal Neuron, neurobiologists Blake Richards and Paul Frankland challenge the usual idea of memory. This idea says that forgetting is a process of losing information, where important details slowly disappear even when we try hard to remember them. Richards and Frankland argue that memory's purpose is not just to store information correctly, but to 'optimize decision-making' in fast-changing situations. In this view, forgetting is a strategy that has developed over time. It is a process that happens in the background of memory, where information that doesn't help us survive is assessed and removed.

items.title: #366 Body Energy
items.answerText: If you've ever had to pick up and carry a tired child through the mall, you know that walking sometimes tuckers out the __toddlers/precursors/doctors/battles__ . Now scientists think they know why. The results appear in the Journal of Experimental Biology. Larger animals tend to use less energy per gram of body __mass/space/tissue/velocity__ than smaller ones do, even at rest. But what happens when they're in motion? Researchers __recruited/advised/dismissed/regretted__ walkers of different ages and sizes, from a three-foot-tall kindergartner to a six-foot adult. While the subjects logged miles on the treadmill, the scientists __measured/presented/microsecond/thickened__ their stride and metabolism. And they found that people pretty much walk the same way, regardless of their stature. If you scaled a five-year-old up to be six-and-a-half feet tall, the giant child would lope along just like a similarly sized adult. What's more, walkers of all heights use the same amount of energy per step. That means that big people don't __conserve/valve/masterworks/slurs__ energy by strolling in a more economical style. They expend less energy because—just as you may have always suspected —they simply need fewer strides to cover the same ground. Which means that for some people a walk in the park ain't necessarily a walk in the park.

The results of their study are in the Journal of Experimental Biology. Larger animals tend to use less energy per gram of body mass than smaller ones, even when they are resting. But what happens when they move?
Researchers studied people of different ages and sizes, from a small kindergartner to a tall adult. The subjects walked on a treadmill while scientists measured their stride and metabolism (how their bodies use energy). The study found that people walk in much the same way, regardless of their height. If a five-year-old were scaled up to be very tall, that child would walk like a similarly sized adult. This results from an understandable fear of the consequences of a real venomous bite. Anxious people may hyperventilate so that they develop pins-and-needles __sensation/movement/sensor/correction__ in the extremities, spasm of their hands and feet, and dizziness. Some may develop vasovagal shock after the bite or suspected bite, with faintness and collapse with profound slowing of the heart. Others may become highly agitated and __irrational/irreparable/motivated/irrigated__ and may manifest a wide range of misleading symptoms. The clinical __presentation/preparation/presence/prediction__ of a snakebite victim varies with the age and size of the patient, the species of snake, the number and location of the bites, and the quantity and toxicity of the venom.

items.title: #368 Yellowstone Bison
items.answerText: Yellowstone is the only place in the United States where bison have lived continuously since prehistoric times. Yellowstone bison are exceptional because they __comprise/congregate/consist/compromise__ the nation’s largest bison population on public land. This population has thousands of individuals that are allowed to roam relatively freely over the expansive landscape of Yellowstone National Park and some nearby areas of Montana. They also __exhibit/disregard/resist/encourage__ wild behavior like their ancient ancestors, congregating during the breeding season to compete for mates, as well as migration and exploration that result in the use of new habitat areas. These behaviors have enabled the successful restoration of a population that was on the __brink/brine/danger/brindle__ of extinction just over a century ago. However, some Yellowstone bison are infected with brucellosis, a livestock disease that can be __transmitted/transplanted/transported/transgressed__ to wild bison and elk as well as to cattle through contact with infected fetal tissue. To prevent conflicts with ranching and other activities outside the park, the National Park Service works with other federal, state, and tribal agencies to manage and develop policies for bison access to __habitat/inhabitant/habitant/food__ in Montana.
items.fullText: Yellowstone is the only place in the United States where bison have lived continuously since prehistoric times. Yellowstone bison are exceptional because they comprise the nation’s largest bison population on public land. This population has thousands of individuals that are allowed to roam relatively freely over the expansive landscape of Yellowstone National Park and some nearby areas of Montana. They also exhibit wild behavior like their ancient ancestors, congregating during the breeding season to compete for mates, as well as migration and exploration that result in the use of new habitat areas. These behaviors have enabled the successful restoration of a population that was on the brink of extinction just over a century ago. However, some Yellowstone bison are infected with brucellosis, a livestock disease that can be transmitted to wild bison and elk as well as to cattle through contact with infected fetal tissue. To prevent conflicts with ranching and other activities outside the park, the National Park Service works with other federal, state, and tribal agencies to manage and develop policies for bison access to habitat in Montana.
items.beginnerText: Yellowstone is the only place in the United States where bison have always lived. Yellowstone bison are special because they are the biggest bison group on public land in the country. Thousands of these bison live freely in Yellowstone National Park and nearby areas of Montana. They act like their ancestors. They gather to find mates. They move around and explore new areas. This has helped the bison population grow again after it almost died out over 100 years ago. But some Yellowstone bison have brucellosis (a disease). This disease can spread to bison, elk, and cows. It spreads when they touch infected tissue. The National Park Service works with other groups to keep bison away from ranches. They make rules about where bison can go in Montana.
items.intermediateText: Yellowstone is unique in the United States as the only location where bison have continuously inhabited the area since prehistoric times. Yellowstone bison are notable for forming the largest bison population on public land in the nation. This population includes thousands of bison that roam freely within Yellowstone National Park and some areas of Montana. They also display wild behaviors similar to their ancestors, such as gathering during the breeding season to compete for mates, and migrating to explore new habitats. These behaviors have allowed this population to recover after almost becoming extinct a century ago. However, some Yellowstone bison carry brucellosis, a livestock disease that can spread to wild bison, elk, and cattle through contact with infected tissue. To avoid problems with ranching and other activities outside the park, the National Park Service collaborates with federal, state, and tribal organizations to manage bison and create policies regarding their access to habitats in Montana.

The homebound folks also had an __increased/repeat/screech/elite__ risk of other cognitive impairments and a faster rate of cognitive decline. Beverley Glover and her team at Cambridge University made some fake flowers. They put sugar water in the flowers. The flowers were kept at different temperatures. items.intermediateText: Many people correctly believe that flowers look the way they do to attract pollinating insects. However, this is not the complete explanation. To rule out the possibility that the color of the fake flowers was a factor, the scientists tested a different color combination and obtained the same result.

CCTV footage – taken from his own security cameras – was again __interpreted/changed/disciplined/dictated__ as key evidence. In most states and territories, children can start full-time schooling at five years old by enrolling in a kindergarten or preparatory year. In 2001, just over half of five-year-olds (57%) were at school, while about a third (34%) attended preschool. Although some states and territories allow children to start preschool before they turn four, the participation rates for three-year-olds are much lower than those for four-year-olds (24% compared with 56% in 2001). items.fullText: World War II played a major role in shaping the direction of communication study during the 1940s. Two instrumental players in communication research during this era, Kurt Lewin and Carl Hovland et al. studied group dynamics and mass communication. Following World War II, scholars such as Lazarsfeld, Lasswell, Hovland, and Schramm wanted to bring more credibility and attention to their research. One approach they used to accomplish this was to call for Communication study to be its own field of research at universities. They began using the terms “mass communication” and “communication research” more frequently in their writings, which helped begin the process of distinguishing Communication research and departments from other fields such as political science, psychology, and sociology. And because I would like to leave this room unlynched, let me amend that to say that at least there should be less of some of it. The reality of science is it takes time for science to play itself out. When interesting new results come in, they're tested and they're confirmed and people rework them. The shift to digital payments also accelerated during the pandemic, leading stores to __replace/exchange/occupy/retrieve__ old-fashioned cash tip jars with tablet touch screens. But these screens and the procedures for digital tipping have proven more intrusive than a low-pressure cash tip jar with a few bucks in it.

The exposed ear allows users to pick up on sounds and the environment around them, crucial for safety when doing activities such as riding a bike or jogging.

items.title: #499 Talent Recruitment
items.answerText: The demand for workers in the US is __outpacing/falling/flipping/irrigating__ the supply, and finding the best talent is going to be increasingly difficult as the world navigates a period of heightened economic uncertainty. In this age of uncertainty, when companies __prioritize/neglect/worsen/alleviate__ skills (not degrees or “who you know”), they can build a more agile workforce that has gained experiences via many different routes, which can help to avoid “group-think” and lead to more dynamic teams. Recognizing the diverse ways skills are acquired and __adopting/distinguishing/digitizing/attempting__ a skills-first approach to talent will bring greater transparency, efficiency and equity to the labor market, making it easier for anyone from anywhere to achieve anything.

items.title: #501 Poverty and Disease
items.answerText: At the Gates Foundation, we believe it’s possible, and __imperative/impaired/impalpable/impressive__ , to invest in long-term, sustainable action, especially after two years of conflict, pandemic and polarization. Rising inflation has affected virtually every nation, reducing countries’ spending power and forcing tough financial trade-offs. An __alarming/unintentional/implicit/absolute__ number of people, particularly women, are hungry worldwide. Many countries are pulling back on development aid that helps strengthen health and food systems over the long term in low and middle income countries. Some have __redirected/rebounded/expended/recouped__ funds from these priorities to address crises at home. Humanitarian aid is critical. Yet if short-term funding means __neglecting/emphasizing/alerting/covering__ long-term investment, health emergencies and food shortages will become even more frequent -- and more intense. Hunger, disease and inequity are problems without borders, and every sector has a role to play in solving them. Solutions can come from everywhere: from the most advanced labs and the most remote communities.

The subject of conservation is broader than this, however. Even a species that survives extinction can lose much of its genetic diversity as local, genetically distinct populations are lost from most of the species’ original range. items.title: #504 Energy Flow
items.answerText: The fundamental source of energy in almost all ecosystems is radiant energy from the Sun. The energy of sunlight is used by the ecosystem’s autotrophic, or self-sustaining, organisms (that is, those that can make their own food). Consisting largely of green vegetation, these organisms are __capable/aware/proud/guilty__ of photosynthesis - i.e., they can use the energy of sunlight to __convert/communicate/build/force__ carbon dioxide and water into simple, energy-rich carbohydrates. The autotrophs use the energy stored within the simple carbohydrates to produce the more __complex/normal/authentic/futile__ organic compounds, such as proteins, lipids, and starches, that maintain the organisms’ life processes. The autotrophic segment of the ecosystem is commonly __referred/made/known/provided__ to as the producer level. Organic matter generated by autotrophs directly or indirectly sustains heterotrophic organisms.

items.title: #506 Water Temperature
items.answerText: Water temperature is an important physical property of every river and stream. Many plants, animals, and other organisms living in streams can __flourish/wither/perish/deteriorate__ only in a specific range of water temperatures. Temperature can affect certain aspects of water quality. For example, higher temperatures reduce levels of dissolved oxygen in the water, which can negatively affect the growth and __productivity/corrosion/appreciation/degradation__ of aquatic life. Construction workers in places such as Hong Kong rely on bamboo scaffolding whatever the height of the tower block they may be working on: over a billion people around the world live in a home that is made of bamboo; and China has cultivated the plant for thousands of years. The only drawback to this remarkable product is the cost of transporting it. So for those who live in cooler regions of the world, the enormous advantages of this natural building material are less accessible.

items.title: #542 Neutrinos
items.answerText: In June 1998, an international team of Japanese and US physicists unveiled strong evidence that elusive subatomic particles known as neutrinos have mass. These findings run __counter/away/towards/forth__ to the standard model of particle physics—the basic theory about the structure of matter—which holds that these electrically neutral, weakly interacting particles have no mass. The discovery means that existing theoretical models of matter must now be __revised/denied/identified/celebrated__ to include neutrinos with mass. Neutrinos occur in three states: electron, muon, and tau, with the names signifying what is produced when a neutrino collides with another particle. __Observers/Respondents/Electrons/Muons__ do not see the neutrinos themselves, but can detect the creation of electrons and muons from faint flashes of light following a particle collision. The physicists used the giant Super-Kamiokande—the world's biggest neutrino detector buried deep underground in Mozumi, Japan. In the experiment, __submerged/destroyed/concealed/revealed__ in a 50,000-ton tank of purified water, neutrinos created when cosmic rays bombard Earth's upper atmosphere were counted relative to the number expected to penetrate the cavern. The experimenters found that the number of electron-neutrinos detected was relatively constant with theorized totals, while the number of muon-neutrinos was significantly lower. This indicated that they were disappearing into another state, or "flavor," such as an undetected tau-neutrino, or possibly another type.

items.intermediateText: In June 1998, an international team of Japanese and US physicists found strong evidence that neutrinos have mass. These subatomic particles had previously been thought to be massless. These findings contradict the standard model of particle physics, which is the basic theory about the structure of matter. This model says that these electrically neutral particles do not have mass. Because of this discovery, current theoretical models of matter must be updated to include neutrinos with mass. Neutrinos exist in three states: electron, muon, and tau. These names indicate what is produced when a neutrino collides with another particle. Scientists cannot see the neutrinos themselves. However, they can detect the creation of electrons and muons from faint flashes of light after a particle collision. The physicists used the Super-Kamiokande, which is the world's largest neutrino detector, located underground in Mozumi, Japan. In the experiment, they used a 50,000-ton tank of purified water. They counted neutrinos created when cosmic rays hit Earth's upper atmosphere. They compared this to the expected number that would penetrate the cavern. The experimenters found that the number of electron-neutrinos detected was close to the expected number. However, the number of muon-neutrinos was much lower. This suggested that they were changing into another state, also called a "flavor," such as an undetected tau-neutrino.

Since the early 1970s, scientists had predicted the existence of hot springs (geothermal vents) at active spreading centers along the mid-oceanic ridges, where magma, at temperatures over 1,000°, was likely erupting to form new oceanic crust. The discovery of abundant and unusual sea life, including giant tube worms, huge clams, and mussels, thriving around the hot springs was even more exciting because it was completely unexpected.

I was assigned to Group Two with another eleven boy and girls who had come from big cities in China. I was told that language study required smallness so that we would each get more attention from the skillful teachers. The better the school, the smaller the class. I realized that my classmates were ready all talking in English, simple sentences tossed out to each other in their red-faced introductions and carefree chatting. Their intonations were curving and dramatic and their pronunciation refined and accurate. But as I stretched to catch the drips and drops of their humming dialogue, I couldn’t understand it all, only that it was English. Those words now flying before me sounded a little familiar. I had read them and tried to speak them, but I had never heard them spoken back to me in such a speedy, fluent manner. My big plan of beating the city folks was thawing before my eyes.

I learned that language classes were small. This way, we got more help from the good teachers. The best schools had the smallest classes. My classmates spoke English well. They used easy sentences to talk to each other. They chatted easily. Their voices went up and down a lot. They spoke clearly. I tried to hear what they said. But I could not understand everything. I only knew it was English. The words sounded a bit like what I knew. I had read them and tried to say them. But I had never heard them spoken so fast. My plan to do better than the city students was failing.
items.intermediateText: In 1983, twenty-six new students started studying English at Beijing Language Institute. I was placed in Group Two with eleven other students who came from large Chinese cities. I was told that language learning needed small classes. This way, we would each receive more attention from the experienced teachers. The better the school, the smaller the class size. I noticed that my classmates were already speaking English easily. They used simple sentences when they introduced themselves and chatted. Their intonation was very expressive, and their pronunciation was accurate. However, as I listened closely to their conversation, I couldn’t understand everything, only that it was English. The words sounded somewhat familiar. I had read them and tried to speak them, but I had never heard them spoken so quickly and fluently. My plan to outperform the city students was starting to fail.

items.title: #562 Job Hunting
items.answerText: When it comes to job-hunting, first impressions are critical. Remember, you are marketing a product - yourself - to a potential employer. The first thing the employer sees when greeting you is your __appearance/make-up/suit/body__ ;thus, you must make every effort to have the proper dress for the type of job you are seeking. Will dressing properly get you the job? Of course not, but it will give you a competitive edge and a __positive/grudging/gratuitous/punctilious__ first impression. Should you be judged by what you wear? Perhaps not, but the reality is, of course, that you are judged. Throughout the entire job-seeking process employers use short-cuts — heuristics or rules of thumb — to save time. With cover letters, it’s the opening paragraph and a quick scan of your qualifications. With resumes, it is a quick scan of your accomplishments. With the job interview, it’s how you’re dressed that sets the __tone/tongue/key/taste__ of the interview. How should you dress? Dressing conservatively is always the safest route, but you should also try and do a little investigating of your __prospective/prosper/proactive/projective__ employer so that what you wear to the interview makes you look as though you __fit/keep/jump/suit__ in with the organization. If you overdress (which is rare but can happen) or under dress (the more likely scenario), the potential employer may feel that you don't care enough about the job.

Dressing conservatively is always the safest route, but you should also try and do a little investigating of your prospective employer so that what you wear to the interview makes you look as though you fit in with the organization. If you overdress (which is rare but can happen) or under dress (the more likely scenario), the potential employer may feel that you don't care enough about the job.

Purple loosestrife (Lythrum salicaria) control has been criticized. People say there is not enough proof that it causes harm. Also, using biocontrol has been criticized. People say there is not enough proof that other control methods have failed. In 1985, there was little proof of harm to wetlands. Now, we know that purple loosestrife changes how things rot and how nutrients move in wetlands. It also reduces plant variety and harms some birds. Drawing on archival data and experimental studies, we show that Olympic athletes (among others) are more likely to make counterfactual comparisons based on their __prior/after/last/before__ expectations, consistent with decision affect theory. items.fullText: In an often-cited study about counterfactuals, Medvec, Madey, and Gilovich (1995) found that bronze medalists appeared happier than silver medalists in television coverage of the 1992 Summer Olympics. Medvec et al argued that bronze medalists compared themselves to 4th place finishers, whereas silver medalists compared themselves to gold medalists. These counterfactuals were the most salient because they were either qualitatively different (gold vs silver) or categorically different (medal vs no medal) from what actually occurred. Drawing on archival data and experimental studies, we show that Olympic athletes (among others) are more likely to make counterfactual comparisons based on their prior expectations, consistent with decision affect theory. Silver medalists are more likely to be disappointed because their personal expectations are higher than those of bronze medalists.

This was seen on TV during the 1992 Summer Olympics. The study said bronze medal winners thought about those who came in 4th place. Silver medal winners thought about the gold medal winners. These comparisons were important because they were very different. It was gold compared to silver, or a medal compared to no medal. The study also showed that Olympic athletes often compare themselves to what they expected before. This is related to decision affect theory. Silver medal winners are often more sad because they expected more.
items.intermediateText: In a well-known study about counterfactuals, Medvec, Madey, and Gilovich (1995) discovered that bronze medalists seemed happier than silver medalists during the 1992 Summer Olympics television coverage. Medvec et al. claimed that bronze medalists compared themselves to those finishing in 4th place, while silver medalists compared themselves to gold medalists. These counterfactuals were the most noticeable because they differed in quality (gold vs. silver) or category (medal vs. no medal) from what actually happened. Using data and experiments, we demonstrate that Olympic athletes often make counterfactual comparisons based on their prior expectations. This aligns with decision affect theory. Silver medalists are more likely to be disappointed because their personal expectations are higher than bronze medalists'.

items.title: #575 Natural Capital

These services include purifying our water, __regulating/guiding/diminishing/denying__ our climate, reducing flood risk, and pollinating our crops. The Natural Capital Project — a partnership __among/between/upon/for__ WWF, The Nature Conservancy, University of Minnesota and Stanford University — works to provide decision makers with __reliable/liable/strong/powerful__ ways to assess the true value of the services that ecosystems provide. An essential element of the Natural Capital Project is developing tools that help decision makers protect biodiversity and ecosystem services.
items.fullText: Capital has often been thought of narrowly as physical capital — the machines, tools, and equipment used in the production of other goods, but our wealth and wellbeing also relies on natural capital. If we forget this, we risk degrading the services that natural ecosystems provide, which support our economies and sustain our lives. These services include purifying our water, regulating our climate, reducing flood risk, and pollinating our crops. The Natural Capital Project — a partnership among WWF, The Nature Conservancy, University of Minnesota and Stanford University — works to provide decision makers with reliable ways to assess the true value of the services that ecosystems provide. An essential element of the Natural Capital Project is developing tools that help decision makers protect biodiversity and ecosystem services.
items.beginnerText: We often think of capital as machines and tools. These are used to make other things. But we also depend on natural capital. If we forget this, we could hurt natural ecosystems. Ecosystems help our economies and lives. They clean our water and control our climate. They also help stop floods and pollinate crops. The Natural Capital Project is a group that includes WWF and other groups. They help leaders find the real value of ecosystems. They also create tools to protect biodiversity and ecosystems.
items.intermediateText: Capital is often seen as physical capital, like machines and tools used to make goods. However, our wealth and wellbeing also depend on natural capital. If we ignore this, we risk damaging the services that natural ecosystems provide, which support our economies and lives. These services include cleaning our water, controlling our climate, reducing flood risk, and pollinating crops. The Natural Capital Project, a partnership including WWF, The Nature Conservancy, University of Minnesota, and Stanford University, helps decision-makers assess the real value of ecosystem services. A key part of their work is creating tools to help decision-makers protect biodiversity and ecosystem services.

items.title: #579 Settlement
items.answerText: Over the last ten thousand years there seem to have been two separate and conflicting building sentiments throughout the history of towns and cities. __One/It/What/That__ is the desire to start again, for a variety of reasons: an earthquake or a tidal wave may have demolished the settlement, or fire destroyed it, or the new city __marks/highlights/starts/protrudes__ a new political beginning. A good example is Currowan, on the Clyde River in New South Wales, which __was surveyed/has been surveyed/had surveyed/be surveyed__ in the second half of the 19th century, in expectation that people would come to establish agriculture and a small port. items.fullText: Over the last ten thousand years there seem to have been two separate and conflicting building sentiments throughout the history of towns and cities. One is the desire to start again, for a variety of reasons: an earthquake or a tidal wave may have demolished the settlement, or fire destroyed it, or the new city marks a new political beginning. The other can be likened to the effect of a magnet: established settlements attract people, who tend to come whether or not there is any planning for their arrival. The clash between these two sentiments is evident in every established city unless its development has been almost completely accidental or is lost in history. Incidentally, many settlements have been planned from the beginning but, for a variety of reasons, no settlement followed the plan. A good example is Currowan, on the Clyde River in New South Wales, which was surveyed in the second half of the 19th century, in expectation that people would come to establish agriculture and a small port. items.beginnerText: For the last ten thousand years, there seem to be two ways of thinking about building towns and cities. One way is to want to start again. This might be because of an earthquake or a flood that destroyed the town. It could also be because of a fire, or because the new city is a new start for politics. The other way is like a magnet. Towns that are already there bring people in. People come even if no one planned for them to come. These two ideas fight each other in every town that has been around for a while. This happens unless the town grew by accident or its history is unknown. Many towns were planned from the start. But for different reasons, no one followed the plan. For example, Currowan in New South Wales was surveyed in the second half of the 19th century. People thought people would come to farm and make a small port. But nobody came.
items.intermediateText: For the past ten thousand years, there appear to be two distinct and opposing ideas about building towns and cities. One is the desire to rebuild, often due to events like earthquakes, tidal waves, or fires that destroyed the previous settlement. It can also be driven by the creation of a new city to mark a new political era. The other idea is similar to the effect of a magnet: existing settlements attract people, regardless of whether their arrival is planned for. The conflict between these two ideas is clear in most established cities, unless their growth was largely unplanned or has been forgotten by history. Interestingly, many settlements were initially planned. However, for various reasons, these plans were never followed. A key example is Currowan, located on the Clyde River in New South Wales. It was surveyed in the second half of the 19th century, with the expectation that people would come to develop agriculture and a small port. However, no one ever settled there.

The Australian Government had been providing regular funding to universities since the late 1950s, but in 1974, it took over full responsibility for funding higher education. At this time, tuition fees were abolished with the aim of making university education affordable for all Australians who were able and willing to participate. Since the late 1980s, there has been a shift towards increased private contributions, particularly from student fees. In 1989, the Australian Government introduced the Higher Education Contribution Scheme (HECS), which included a loan scheme to help students finance their education. This allowed universities to remain accessible by allowing students to delay payments until they could afford to pay off their loans. items.title: #582 Economics

In practice, resources can __encompass/trespass/surpass/debate__ everything from time to knowledge and property to tools. As such, economics helps illustrate how people interact within the market to __realize/idolize/utilize/finalize__ their diverse goals. Beyond defining what these resources are, the concept of scarcity is also an important consideration. These resources — no matter how broad the category — are limited, which is the source of tension in the choices people and society make: Their decisions are a result of the __constant/resonant/extant/blatant__ tug of war between unlimited wants and desires and limited resources.
items.fullText: Economics is the study of choices. Though some believe that economics is driven purely by money or capital, the choice is much more expansive . If the study of economics is the study of how people choose to use their resources, analysts must also consider all of their possible resources, of which money is but one. In practice, resources can encompass everything from time to knowledge and property to tools. As such, economics helps illustrate how people interact within the market to realize their diverse goals. Beyond defining what these resources are, the concept of scarcity is also an important consideration. These resources — no matter how broad the category — are limited, which is the source of tension in the choices people and society make: Their decisions are a result of the constant tug of war between unlimited wants and desires and limited resources.
items.beginnerText: Economics is about studying choices. Some people think economics is only about money. But choices are bigger than just money. Economics looks at how people use what they have. This means looking at all the things people can use, not just money. People can use time, knowledge, things they own, and tools. So, economics shows how people work together to get what they want. It also looks at scarcity. Scarcity means there is not enough of everything. People must choose because they want many things, but there is only so much available.
items.intermediateText: Economics is the study of choices. Although some believe economics focuses only on money or capital, the scope is much broader. If economics studies how people use their resources, analysts must consider all possible resources, of which money is only one. In reality, resources include everything from time and knowledge to property and tools. Therefore, economics helps explain how people interact in the market to achieve their various goals. In addition to defining resources, scarcity is an important idea. These resources, however broad, are limited. This creates tension in the choices people and society make. Their decisions result from the constant struggle between unlimited wants and limited resources.

These institutions may vary from culture to culture, particularly in traditional societies versus modern societies. In larger traditional societies, carpentry, stonemasonry, and shipbuilding are also prominent. items.beginnerText: We can find the history of vaccines back to the 7th century. At that time, monks in India tried to protect themselves from illness. They did this by drinking snake venom. The first vaccine was using human smallpox. People in India, Arabia, and China did this a lot. This vaccine worked by taking pus from someone with a mild case of smallpox. Then, they put the pus into a healthy person. This caused a small infection. A Greek man named Timoni brought this idea to England. But, this method could spread smallpox. It could also make the person who got the pus sicker. Using human smallpox was not agreed on by everyone. In 1796, Jenner made a vaccine from cow smallpox. This new method also had problems, but people kept using it. Smallpox could be stopped by using pus from someone with cowpox. Jenner called this substance "vaccine." items.intermediateText: According to research, the history of vaccination goes back to the 7th century. At that time, monks in India attempted to protect themselves from diseases by drinking snake venom. The first type of vaccination involved inoculation with human smallpox, a method used in ancient India, Arabia, and China. This vaccination method involved taking pus from a patient with a mild smallpox infection and introducing it to a healthy person, which then caused a minor infection. A Greek man named Timoni first introduced this method in England. However, this method carried the risk of spreading smallpox within the community and potentially worsening the health of the person being inoculated. While using human smallpox vaccine was debated, Jenner developed a bovine smallpox vaccine in 1796. This new method also faced controversy but became more widespread. Smallpox became preventable by injecting pus taken from a person infected with cowpox. Jenner named the substance "vaccine" after the Latin word "vacca," meaning "cow," which is how the process of giving a vaccine became known as "vaccination."

items.intermediateText: Want to know what will make you happy? A new study from Harvard University suggests asking a complete stranger. Gilbert states, “If you want to know how much you will enjoy an experience, you are better off knowing how much someone else enjoyed it.” He suggests that instead of imagining the future, we should look at the experiences of others. Previous research shows that people struggle to predict their own preferences, which leads to poor decisions. Attempts to improve the accuracy of these predictions have generally failed.

Ether (used from 1846) induced complete unconsciousness and had a long-lasting effect. Yet, it could cause coughing during operations and sickness afterward. Additionally, it was highly flammable and came in heavy glass bottles. Chloroform (used from 1847) proved very effective with minimal side effects. Nevertheless, determining the correct dosage was challenging, and it could be fatal to some individuals due to its effect on the heart. An inhaler assisted in controlling the dosage.

Today, people worry that kids spend too much time doing quiet things. Many kids do not get enough exercise each day (60 minutes of active exercise). This can cause more kids to be overweight. Watching TV and playing computer games are quiet activities. Kids spend 2.5–4 hours a day doing these things.
"Active video games" (AVGs) are new. They can turn quiet screen time into active screen time. This can help kids use more energy. AVGs use cameras and sensors. Kids can move their bodies in different ways, like playing tennis or running. The best AVGs are like walking. They are low-intensity activities. AVGs are better than quiet games. items.intermediateText:
There is concern about children spending more time on sedentary activities. Many children do not meet the daily recommendations for physical activity (60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity). This lack of activity may be linked to rising obesity rates. Activities like watching television and playing computer games are common sedentary pastimes. Children spend about 2.5–4 hours each day on these activities.
"Active video games" (AVGs) offer a chance to change sedentary screen time into active time, which can increase daily energy use. AVGs use cameras and sensors. This allows players to physically perform actions, like swinging a tennis racket or running, depending on the game. The most intense AVGs are similar to walking and are considered low-intensity activities. AVGs are a better option than sedentary gaming. However, they are not enough to replace regular physical activity, such as sports and outdoor play.

items.fullText: A crime is generally a deliberate act that results in harm, physical or otherwise, toward one or more people, in a manner prohibited by law. The determination of which acts are to be considered criminal has varied historically ,and continues to do so among cultures and nations. When a crime is committed, a process of discovery ,trial by judge or jury, conviction, and punishment occurs. Just as what is considered criminal varies between jurisdictions ,so does the punishment, but elements of restitution and deterrence are common.

What is seen as a crime has changed over time. It is also different in different countries and cultures. When someone does a crime, there is an investigation. items.title: #621 Fluid Behavior
items.answerText: If you see a movie, or a TV advertisement, that involves a fluid behaving in an unusual way, it was probably made using technology based on the work of a Monash researcher. These fast-moving, lightweight animals live in the rainforests of South America. Their small size makes it easy for them to dart about the trees, catching insects and small animals such as lizards, frogs, and snails. Marmosets have another unusual food source - they use their chisel-like incisor teeth to dig into tree bark and lap up the gummy sap that seeps out, leaving telltale, oval-shaped holes in the branches when they have finished. items.title: #634 Seatbelt
items.answerText: I am a cyclist and a motorist. I fasten my seatbelt when I drive and wear a helmet on my bike to reduce the risk of injury. I am convinced that these are prudent safety measures. I have persuaded many friends to wear helmets on the grounds that transplant surgeons call those without helmets, "donors on wheels". But a book on ‘Risk' by my colleague John Adams has made me re-examine my deeply held __convictions/conviction/minds/obsessions__ . Adams has completely __undermined/underestimated/understood/underwent__ my confidence in these apparently sensible precautions. What he has persuasively argued, particularly in relation to seat belts, is that the evidence that they do what they are supposed to do is very suspect. This is __in spite of/because of/in contrast with/in terms of__ numerous claims that seat belts save many thousands of lives every year. There is remarkable data on the years 1970 and 1978 in which countries where seat belts are __compulsory/recommended/approved/accepted__ have had on average about 5 per cent more road accident deaths following the introduction of the law. In the UK, road deaths have decreased steadily from about 7,000 a year in 1972 to just over 4,000 in 1989. There is no evidence in the trend for any effect of the seat belt law that was introduced in 1983. Moreover, there is evidence that the number of cyclists and pedestrians killed actually increased by about 10 per cent.

This represents a strong average annual growth of 6.5 per cent. This paper analyzes the demand for outbound travel to various countries, using travel demand models focused on short-term resident departures. The models are based on a double logarithmic linear functional form. Overseas departures are the dependent variable, while real household disposable income, travel and accommodation prices in both Australia and overseas, and the exchange rate serve as independent variables. These models were estimated using historical time series data from 1973 to 1998, sourced from organizations such as the World Tourism Organization, the Australian Bureau of Statistics, the World Bank, and the International Monetary Fund. The number of short-term resident departures is positively influenced by per capita real household disposable income and the price of domestic travel and accommodation. items.title: #641 History of Sociology
items.answerText: Although sociology has its roots in the works of philosophers like Plato, Aristotle, and Confucius, it is a relatively new academic discipline. It __emerged/traversed/survived/invented__ in the early 19th century in response to the challenges of modernity. The impact of this exposure was varied, but for some people, it included the breakdown of traditional norms and customs and __warranted/unwarranted/transplanted/implanted__ a revised understanding of how the world works. Thinkers of the Enlightenment period in the 18th century also helped set the __stage/rule/standard/tone__ for the sociologists who would follow. items.fullText: The emperor is the giant of the penguin world and the most iconic of the birds of Antarctica. Gold patches on their ears and on the top of their chest brighten up their black heads. Emperors and their closest relative, the king penguin, have unique breeding cycles, with very long chick-rearing periods. The emperor penguins breed the furthest south of any penguin species, forming large colonies on the sea-ice surrounding the Antarctic continent. They are true Antarctic birds, rarely seen in the subantarctic waters. So that the chicks can fledge in the late summer season, emperors breed during the cold, dark winter, with temperatures as low at - 50°C and winds up to 200 km per hour. They live in big groups on the ice around Antarctica. They live only in Antarctica and are rarely seen in other areas. Emperor penguins breed in the cold, dark winter. This is so their young can grow up in the late summer. It can be very cold, about -50°C, and the wind can blow up to 200 km per hour. They walk 50–120 km (30–75 mls) on the ice to breed. Many penguins stay together. The female lays one egg in May. Then, she gives the egg to the male to keep warm. She goes to the sea to eat. For nine weeks, the male does not eat. items.intermediateText: The emperor penguin is the largest penguin and a well-known symbol of Antarctica. They have gold markings on their ears and upper chest, which add brightness to their black heads. Emperor penguins, along with their close relatives the king penguins, have unique breeding cycles characterized by lengthy chick-rearing periods. Emperor penguins breed further south than any other penguin species, gathering in large colonies on the sea ice around Antarctica. These penguins are truly Antarctic and are rarely found in subantarctic waters. Emperor penguins breed during the cold, dark winter to ensure their chicks can mature by late summer. Temperatures can drop to -50°C, with winds reaching up to 200 km per hour. They travel 50–120 km (30–75 mls) across the ice to reach breeding colonies that can include thousands of penguins. In May, the female lays a single egg and then transfers it to the male for incubation, while she goes to the sea to feed. For nine weeks, the male fasts, losing 45% of his body weight. He balances the egg on his feet, which are covered by a thick layer of skin and feathers. The temperature of the egg can be 70°C higher than the outside air temperature.

Also, we should not change our code to make a site look the same on every browser. Instead, we give all users the main functions and information. Then, we make the site look and work better for users with better browsers. This is a good way to develop websites. We don't spend hours trying to add effects to every browser. items.fullText: Over many centuries and across many territories the Romans were able to win an astonishing number of military victories and their success was due to several important factors. Italy was a peninsula not easily attacked. There was a huge pool of fighting men to draw upon, a disciplined and innovative army, a centralized command and line of supply, expert engineers, effective diplomacy through a network of allies, and an inclusive approach to conquered people, which allowed for strengthening and broadening of the Roman power and logistical bases. Further , her allies not only supplied, equipped and paid for additional men but they also supplied vital materials such as grain and ships.
